items.title: NVIDIA and Paradromics Want Brain Implants to Keep Up With Conversation
items.summary: A Paradromics trial participant used a brain implant to talk with her grandchildren. Now the company is working with NVIDIA on the computing that could make those conversations easier to have every day.
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

NVIDIA and Paradromics Want Brain Implants to Keep Up With Conversation

A Paradromics trial participant used a brain implant to talk with her grandchildren. Now the company is working with NVIDIA on the computing that could make those conversations easier to have every day.

Written By
Corey Noles
Nov 23, 2026
· 3 minute read

“Okay, I have a lot to say.”

That’s what the first participant in Paradromics’ brain-implant study chose to say when researchers switched on a mode that let her use her own words. She later used the system to talk with her grandchildren on a live phone call, according to Paradromics’ September study update.

Now Paradromics is teaming up with NVIDIA to tackle what happens between the moment someone tries to speak and the moment everyone else hears them. The collaboration will start with speech restoration, with the goal of making the AI respond faster, adapt as brain signals change, and eventually run on smaller hardware.

That matters because conversation has terrible manners. People jump in, talk over each other, and take a pause as an invitation to change the subject. Getting the words right matters. Getting them out in time to take your turn matters, too.

Two ways to turn brain signals into speech

Advertisement

Paradromics’ investigational Connexus implant records electrical activity from neurons. A decoder learns to map patterns in that activity to signals associated with speech. Paradromics plans to move its speech decoders and voice synthesis software onto NVIDIA’s platform for processing live sensor data, Holoscan. The collaboration will also use NVIDIA’s compact Jetson computing hardware.

The companies are pursuing two approaches. One goes directly from neural activity to synthesized speech. The other decodes the activity into text, uses a language model in that process, and then reads the text aloud. The roadmap sets targets of under 10 milliseconds for computing and moving data in the direct system and under 100 milliseconds for the text-first system. Those are engineering targets. The time someone actually waits to hear intelligible speech is a separate measure.

There’s a reason to explore the direct route beyond speed. In a 2025 UC Davis study, a man with ALS used a separate experimental brain-to-voice system to vary his pitch, emphasize words, and even sing simple melodies. The synthesized speech varied in intelligibility, but he could raise his pitch to make a sentence sound like a question. Plain text leaves much of that up to the voice synthesizer. Read the UC Davis study.

Advertisement

Paradromics also wants its models to recalibrate in the background while someone uses the device. A decoder learns what a person’s neural signals look like when they try to speak. As those patterns change, the model has to keep up. If background adjustment works, users could spend less time retraining the system and more time using it.

NVIDIA is making a play for the computer outside the implant

Paradromics plans to give academic partners in its APEX research program NVIDIA IGX and Holoscan-ready systems. The idea is to let labs test new applications on a common setup without rebuilding the computing infrastructure each time. Speech comes first. The 2027 roadmap adds finer motor control and models that can use visual context to help translate a user’s intent into physical action.

There’s a familiar NVIDIA strategy here. Brain-interface developer Synchron announced plans to use Holoscan in 2025, and NVIDIA has been pushing its edge computing platforms into fields like medical devices and surgical robotics. If more labs build around the same tools, NVIDIA can become a supplier to the field even as researchers take different approaches to designing implants.

For Paradromics, the next steps are to move the speech software over, measure how much power it draws, and get it into researchers’ hands. Connexus remains investigational, and the Connect-One early feasibility study is gathering preliminary safety data. The longer-term goal is a smaller, lighter external computer that can support all-day use. The test that will matter to someone using it is simple to picture. Can they get a word in at dinner, and can they do it again tomorrow without setting everything up from scratch?

Advertisement

  • Meta is exploring a different route to communication with Brain2Qwerty, a system that decodes brain activity into text without an implant.

items.title: 🎙️ How I AI: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance
items.summary: OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer) Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: Parallel —Web search built for AI scale GiveDirectly —Send cash to the world’s poorest Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of…
items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.contentHtml:
OpenClaw for executives: Automate every 1% annoyance | Ankit Maheshwari (Innovaccer)

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • Parallel—Web search built for AI scale

  • GiveDirectly—Send cash to the world’s poorest

Ankit Maheshwari is the CTO of Innovaccer and the creator of a personal AI chief of staff he runs through OpenClaw on a Mac Mini. In this episode, he shows how his Jarvis handles work approvals, orders lunch, calls coworkers who miss Slack messages, books restaurants, and controls his smart home. He also explains how he uses soul files, specialist subagents, and strict guardrails to make the system trustworthy, and why he is testing local models against a $500 to $600 monthly Anthropic bill.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The best reason to stick with an agent platform is control, not habit. Ankit remains on OpenClaw because it can use his credentials, act on his behalf, and complete tasks without requesting permission at every step. That autonomy is an architectural advantage, not brand loyalty.

  2. Start with the bottleneck, not the grand vision. Ankit’s first automation was a cron job that runs every four hours and briefs him on every resume awaiting approval, including candidate pedigree and GitHub history. Once it worked, he began spotting similar bottlenecks throughout his day.

  3. Specialized agents outperform generalist ones once the workload becomes complex. Ankit’s master agent struggled to maintain the right persona across restaurant bookings and coworker check-ins. Moving voice calls to a dedicated agent improved consistency and clarified the split between orchestration and execution.

  4. Configuring soul files requires more work than integrations. The hardest part was defining each agent’s personality, boundaries, permissions, and routing logic through files such as soul.md. Getting those instructions right required more iteration than connecting the underlying tools.

  5. Guardrails should cover the worst case before it happens. OpenClaw once approved expiring travel requests while Ankit was in transit, using the same budget and customer-impact criteria he would have applied. The decisions were sound, but the experience exposed other actions, such as job-role approvals, that needed explicit limits.

  6. The model bill is worth optimizing before the system becomes indispensable. Jarvis costs Ankit roughly $500 to $600 per month on Opus 5.5. Early tests suggest a nearly free local model can handle summaries, email, cron checks, and call orchestration, while complex browser work still requires a frontier model.

  7. The “1% annoyance” rule is an effective way to discover automations. If a task is even slightly frustrating and repeats a few times, Ankit automates it. That approach led to agents for lunch ordering, unanswered Slack messages, home automation, and potentially even calling the elevator.

  8. A terminal-first approach can keep agent building surprisingly simple. Ankit set up OpenClaw by opening its terminal interface and speaking to it like a new employee. When coding was required, OpenClaw launched Claude Code and managed the implementation itself.

  9. Teach agents the messy details, then let them keep learning. Ankit’s lunch agent confirms his order at 9:30 a.m. and acts independently if he does not respond. After one correction about ordering curry without bread, it learned both when to add bread and when a meal already includes it.

items.title: Jensen Huang Is Back. Nvidia Is Stronger With Him at the Helm.
items.summary: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a unanimous board reversal and a 23% weekly stock plunge. I’m bullish on what his return means for Nvidia as cloud giants build their own chips and customers get serious about what it costs to run AI.
items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Jensen Huang Is Back. Nvidia Is Stronger With Him at the Helm.

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after a unanimous board reversal and a 23% weekly stock plunge. I’m bullish on what his return means for Nvidia as cloud giants build their own chips and customers get serious about what it costs to run AI.

Written By
Corey Noles
Nov 23, 2026
· 4 minute read

Nvidia’s board spent last Tuesday telling investors it had no intention of bringing Jensen Huang back. On Monday, Nvidia announced that the board had unanimously reinstated him as president, CEO, and a director. The decision took effect Sunday, Nov. 22, according to Nvidia’s SEC filing. Colette Kress will continue as CFO, and Harvey Jones will remain board chair, Nvidia said.

I’m bullish on Nvidia with Huang back. When he stepped down, I argued that Nvidia would probably be fine without him. The company had the team and technology to keep executing. Its next challenge is deciding where to push that advantage as customers get more selective about what they spend on AI. I’d rather have Huang making those calls.

The comeback follows Nvidia’s worst week since 2008

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on Nov. 12. He had acknowledged an affair, and the board had opened an independent investigation after reports that he may have been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Jones told investors last Tuesday that Huang had stepped down after disclosing conduct that fell short of company standards. That was also when Jones said the board didn’t intend to reinstate him.

Advertisement

Nvidia shares fell 23% last week, their worst week since October 2008. They dropped about 14% on Friday alone, as a broader tech sell-off deepened and Reuters reported that the SEC was examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. All of that happened in the same week Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% year over year. The company more than doubled sales and still ended the week down nearly a quarter.

Shortly after Monday’s opening bell, Nvidia shares were up about +30% and the Nasdaq Composite was up 6%, the Associated Press reported.

Where Huang gives Nvidia an edge

The strongest argument for bringing Huang back is the business he built around the GPU. Nvidia sells the chips, the networking that lets thousands of them work together, and the software developers use to make the whole system run. That gives it several ways to lower what customers pay to run a model. A faster chip helps. So does better software that gets more work out of the same rack. Nvidia is betting on both with Vera Rubin.

Rubin brought in nearly $20 billion in its first quarter of production shipments, Kress told investors last week. That gives Huang a platform customers are already buying at scale as he makes the case for what it costs to run AI on Nvidia hardware.

That matters as more of the AI bill comes from running models day after day. If you’re paying to run an AI agent millions of times, the cost of each run can decide whether the product makes money. A cloud provider can keep buying Nvidia GPUs for some jobs and move others to its own chips. Google is already offering customers more ways to use its custom TPUs. Huang’s job is to make the case for Nvidia one workload at a time, and his track record of getting chips, software, and customers moving together is why I like the company’s chances.

Advertisement

The board has work to do, too. Nvidia said it received input from senior U.S. officials before the vote and that its independent investigation will continue. President Donald Trump endorsed the reinstatement Monday and said the government had no reason to believe Huang’s return posed a national security risk, the Associated Press reported.

Huang is due to sit for a transcribed interview with three House committees on Dec. 1, with Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter scheduled for Dec. 2, the committee chairs said.

Nvidia is also hiring a chief compliance officer who will report to a board committee. The board owes employees and shareholders a clear account of what the investigation finds and how it will enforce its standards. Meanwhile, the commercial headaches are real. Nvidia recently halted licensed H200 shipments to China despite U.S. approval.

The next phase of AI infrastructure is going to be won contract by contract, as buyers figure out which workloads are worth running at scale and what they can afford to pay for them. Nvidia enters that fight with an enormous lead and the founder who built it. That’s a stronger position than the one it was in on Friday.

Advertisement

Related Reading

  • Our original analysis of the leadership crisis explains what Kress inherited and why Nvidia’s software and customer relationships gave it room to weather the shock. Jensen Huang Resigns. Nvidia Will Probably Be Fine—Eventually.
  • The H200 episode shows how much uncertainty Nvidia faces even after Washington approves a chip sale. Why Did Nvidia Stop Selling AI Chips to China After Getting U.S. Approval?
  • Huawei’s hardware and DeepSeek’s software show how competitors are trying to make it easier for developers to switch away from Nvidia. DeepSeek Opened the Code. Can Huawei Deliver the Compute?

items.title: What happens when AI splits up your friend group?
items.summary: In San Francisco, Julie Krafchick, co-host of “ The Psychology of Relationships ,” was working on podcast episodes and researching how people connect , but still keeping up with friends in media and tech. In some friend circles, you were falling behind if you weren’t using AI…
items.author: Elise Leise
items.contentHtml:
In San Francisco, Julie Krafchick, co-host of “The Psychology of Relationships,” was working on podcast episodes and researching how people connect, but still keeping up with friends in media and tech. In some friend circles, you were falling behind if you weren’t using AI models to “10x” your life and work. In others, dinner talk consisted of debates over whether The New York Times or Granta had published AI-generated work. 

Krafchick was torn. On one hand, she could see AI’s potential; she’d had a career in tech. But in both circles, she found herself deliberating how and when to talk about AI. In one exchange, a friend told her how her latest Claude project was something she had “put her heart and soul” into. 

But Krafchick didn’t necessarily view AI that way. “Personally, I want to do [creative] work,” she told Big Think. “I want to get my hands wet. So there can be a divide…when it almost feels like your friend is taking a shortcut.” Part of her felt she had worked for years to master the craft, only to have someone else “put in a prompt.” 

Still, it felt a bit dramatic to question her friend’s choice. “I do feel like this is something that…does feel like an off-limits topic,” she added. “You wonder: Why am I getting upset about AI and someone using it?” 

A new taboo

If you’ve ever felt like AI is a fraught topic, you’re not alone. You likely have at least one connection who, by virtue of their age, occupation, or feelings about the tech industry, disagrees strongly with your stance on artificial intelligence. Although AI use continues to rise, a Bentley-Gallup survey from July found that, compared with recent years, more Americans now say AI causes more harm than good, especially young adults, who are roughly split on the issue. 

Fundamentally, these friendship disagreements make sense. Like finance, politics, or sex, AI is one of those topics that holds a multitude of sensitive spots underneath. Did you study for a decade in a field threatened by AI? Are you jealous of your friend who’s set to make millions? Do you hate its use of environmental resources? Are you heavily invested in AI stocks? Often, a theoretical “AI” conversation rapidly triggers personal, practical feelings about its impact. 

Complicating things, friends may cover up their use of AI, depending on the degree to which they think others will accept it. As Sarah Newman, Director of Art & Education at Harvard University’s metaLAB, discovered when she started collecting anonymous confessions from strangers, more people than you may think have “guilty AI secrets,” or ways in which they use AI they don’t feel comfortable fully admitting in public. Should you ask your friend if they generated your wedding speech? What happens if you receive an AI-written apology text? And what if you’re ethically opposed to the AI industry and your friend goes to work at Anthropic? 

Most of the time, friends stay quiet. Even though there are plenty of reasons why AI use is such a high-tension topic — environmental ethics, copyright, and AI layoffs, to name a few — “it almost feels weird,” Krafchick explained, “to confront it.” 

Overrelying on AI

Thanks to her podcast, Krafchick is on the front lines of AI-related friendship debates. For one, AI-mediated advice is making it hard to disagree without behind-the-scenes influence. Friends turn to chatbots to talk through conflicts in friend groups, or even forward AI transcript logs to prove their point. “You’ve probably seen that before with friend groups,” she told Big Think. “People…will just copy and paste.” It’s that sense of: “Claude told me this, so it must be right.” 

As Yael Schonbrun, a clinical psychologist and the author of Why Don’t You Understand Me? The Surprising Science Behind Connecting in a World of Missed Signals, explained that heavy AI use between friends can ultimately chip away at both authenticity and trust. When we use LLMs to edit and “make what we say and think kind of refined,” she pointed out, we risk losing the vulnerability that makes a friendship work. 

Other times, friends may turn to AI to smooth over a conflict, especially if a situation is tense and they don’t know what to say. Asking a friend whether they used AI to craft a message is uncomfortable, but so is not knowing. “When you get a text that almost feels overly polished,” Krafchick told Big Think, “you’re like, ‘Did AI write this or did you write this?’” 

Not everyone, of course, wants to automate friendship. “Some of the best parts of friendship are the wildly inefficient/random/silly texts,” Meagan Phelan, a communications director at Science Journals & Publishing, wrote in response to the launch of AI-integrated text messages. She chalked the value of thoughtful check-ins up to intention, noting that taking away those tiny moments is “a very efficient way to become worse at being a friend.” 

Over time, consistently using AI to communicate can alienate and divide friend groups, especially if one or more people feel like their friends aren’t putting in personal effort. “There’s a larger conversation we need to have,” Schonbrun said, “about the way that AI fits into our relationships.” 

But friendship breakups can’t be the only way forward. So what might it take to get past our initial discomfort and have better conversations? 

A more constructive debate 

Part of the answer seems to be interrogating our own assumptions, taking time to articulate our viewpoints, and leading with curiosity rather than judgment. 

While an AI model can help us understand a friend’s point of view or express our feelings less confrontationally, Krafchick pointed out, from a friendship perspective, it’s typically best to avoid letting AI provide a word-for-word script. If “one friend goes to AI…and then they figure out what to say to the second because AI has given them [the exact words],” she elaborated, that’s when the debate starts to feel “disingenuous.” 

Instead, Schonbrun and Krafchick suggest we approach the conversation with our own words, and get curious. If you disagree, why does your friend feel that way? Are there any potential areas of overlap? What have they read or watched that they think best explains their reasoning behind a take? What’s been their personal experience? And finally — if you ever want to talk about it in a social context — what are their boundaries and how would they like to talk about it? 

In Krafchick’s friend group, the choice isn’t “AI or no AI” so much as it is chatting with the friends she’s with about ideas that catch their interest. Sometimes that’s AI; sometimes it’s not. If she’s at Sunday brunch, she might be fascinated by conversations about how AI might shape relationships moving forward, but less so by talk centered on building agents. “It’s finding what topic within AI makes sense for you,” she added.

While AI models are increasingly used as both advisor and friend, Schonbrun explained, they don’t replace the intimacy of a real friendship. If anything, they create a false expectation of how friendships — the kind that challenge and inspire us — are supposed to work. “We need to have a stake in the game in order for relationships to have depth,” she told Big Think. “For them to grow, [and] for us to be able to grow along with them.”

This article What happens when AI splits up your friend group? is featured on Big Think.

items.author: Corey Noles
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

😺 OpenAI wants AI labs to agree on limits

Written By
Corey Noles
Co-Authors
Corey Noles
Eric Gerard Ruiz
Corey Noles
Nov 23, 2026
· 8 minute read

Welcome, humans.

So apparently The Binding of Isaac had a rough weekend. The Verge reported Sunday that developer Nicalis removed AI-generated music after players found Suno metadata in the game’s tracks. Suno generates music with AI; metadata is the hidden label inside a file that can reveal where it came from. Turns out the receipts were in the audio the whole time. For anyone shipping creative work: files remember, fans check, and admitting you should’ve disclosed AI gets a lot harder after the backlash.

MONDAY AI News, Rumors & the Week Ahead LIVE @ 1:15pm CT!

Did Claude really help crack one of math’s biggest mysteries? Join Corey live this afternoon for AI News, Rumors & the Week Ahead as we unpack the stunning Riemann Hypothesis breakthrough, Anthropic’s record-shattering IPO and its rocky aftermath, and why Signal is fighting to keep AI agents out of your private conversations.

Here’s what happened in AI today:

  • 😺 OpenAI's chief scientist proposed shared limits for frontier AI.

  • 📰 Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute for $4.5B.

  • 📰 OpenRouter removed three providers after data-handling findings.

  • 🍪 Gemini's image tools edit photos and make looping GIFs.

  • 🎓 How to give your coding agent a complete handoff.

... and a whole lot more that you can read about here.

OpenAI’s Chief Scientist Wants Every AI Lab to Agree on Shared Speed Limits

Okay, so on Sunday OpenAI's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, published a post with a proposal that sounds more like arms control than a blog entry. Frontier AI labs, he says, should agree on "common limits," meaning capability thresholds that nobody crosses until they hit concrete milestones for monitoring and understanding what their models are doing. As a first step, OpenAI is publishing its own internal measurements, even though they reveal competitive information.

The measurement he wants everyone to use is called perplexity (no relation to the search company). The idea is simple. Show a model text it hasn't seen, and score how well it predicts each next token, which is roughly the next word or word fragment. A model that's rarely surprised gets a lower score, and lower is better. OpenAI tracks the log of that number, also called cross-entropy loss. Think golf: the score goes down as the models get smarter.

Why that number? Pachocki frames modern AI as a giant predictor trained on huge piles of data. Prompting, finetuning, and reinforcement learning then bring out what that predictor can do. He treats the predictor's score, measured at the end of pretraining, as the best indicator of its underlying ability.

Here's the scoreboard OpenAI shared, measured on its own main internal codebase dataset:

  • GPT-3.5 scored about 0.99, enough for fluent conversation and the original ChatGPT.

  • GPT-4 scored about 0.91, the point where chain-of-thought reasoning (a model working through steps before answering) started to pay off.

  • Below 0.8 is where Pachocki says transformative abilities in cybersecurity and mathematics begin to emerge.

  • Around 0.76 is when OpenAI's models began producing notable results on open math problems.

  • Around 0.68 to 0.7 is the next range, where he expects more transformative abilities but says he doesn't know which.

He also suggests AI-assisted research on pretraining methods could trigger a sudden acceleration, possibly as early as 2027. 2027 starts in about five weeks, for the record.

Pachocki is upfront about the weak spots. Labs use different datasets and training mixes, so comparing across labs is hard. Perplexity doesn't map to any single task people care about. Reasoning is a bigger problem: chain-of-thought greatly boosts capability without lowering perplexity, so a limit built only on this number would miss those gains. He also expects safety tooling to weaken, with alignment audits degrading and models becoming more aware of when they're being tested or trained.

Why this matters: The interesting part is who's asking. A lab at the front of the race is proposing shared limits, and putting its own numbers on the table first. It's still a proposal, not an agreement, and the metric has the gaps above. Two things are worth watching: whether other labs publish their own perplexity numbers, and what the "understanding" milestone turns out to be. Pachocki's example is a successor to chain-of-thought monitors, the tools that read a model's reasoning to catch problems. The limits only mean something if labs agree on what counts as reaching it.

FROM OUR PARTNERS

State of Product reveals what AI still hasn’t solved

80% of product professionals say AI helps them ship faster, but customers aren’t seeing value any sooner. Atlassian’s State of Product 2027 explores the gains AI is delivering and the challenges that remain, from decision-making that hasn’t kept pace to gut instinct overriding customer evidence.

Read the report

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Give your coding agent a complete handoff

Picture a coding agent that says "done," and a chunk of what it calls done doesn't work. That's roughly what researchers found when they built SWE-CoWork, a test that treats coding agents like new hires. Each of its 101 assignments starts with a short handoff, and the real requirements are scattered across 26 simulated colleagues and workplace records, some of them conflicting. The agent has to track them down, sort out the conflicts, and build the thing. Private tests then check the result.

Across 11 models, the top two passed about 63% of the key tests (fail-to-pass tests, meaning tests that fail before the change and should pass after). But they fully completed fewer than 8% of assignments. And 31% of the requirements agents reported as finished failed their tests.

Here's the twist. Handing over every requirement upfront lifted test scores by roughly 16 points for two of the models, but full task success didn't budge. A passing piece of work and a finished assignment are different things. The authors point to requirement tracking as the hard part, from asking questions through building, checking, and handing off. In one example, a model asked the right colleague first 93% of the time but collected only 64% of the requirements that person held. Questions that got put off were often never followed up.

So a better brief helps, but it isn't the fix. The fix is making the agent hold itself to a checklist. Fair warning: this is a simulated workplace, not your repo, and the paper doesn't test this exact prompt. It's our adaptation of the failure pattern.

  1. Put the desired outcome, constraints, and acceptance checks in one place before you delegate.

  2. Ask the agent to list requirements and flag anything ambiguous before it changes code.

  3. Afterward, make it show how it verified each requirement and name anything unfinished. 

Before making changes, list the requirements, constraints, and acceptance checks in my brief. Flag anything ambiguous. Afterward, show how you verified each requirement and identify anything unfinished.

AI is moving faster than oversight. Only 39% of Fortune 100 boards have AI oversight, and companies like Air Canada, Zillow, and Deloitte have already seen what that gap can cost.

items.title: OpenAI Says AI Could Help Build Better AI by 2027. How Close Are We?
items.summary: OpenAI believes AI could begin discovering better ways to train future models as early as 2027. Its latest research shows agents completing increasingly complex tasks, although major breakthroughs in AI-assisted model development remain unproven.
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

OpenAI Says AI Could Help Build Better AI by 2027. How Close Are We?

OpenAI believes AI could begin discovering better ways to train future models as early as 2027. Its latest research shows agents completing increasingly complex tasks, although major breakthroughs in AI-assisted model development remain unproven.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 23, 2026
· 4 minute read

OpenAI thinks something pretty big could happen in 2027: AI might start helping researchers invent better AI.

In a November 22 essay, OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki predicted that AI could soon help discover new ways to train future models. He bases his reasoning on something his team has already seen in mathematics, where AI began solving problems that had puzzled researchers for years.

If the same thing happens in AI development, researchers could discover better training methods much faster. And those improvements could eventually lead to more capable models across science and software development.

  • Why OpenAI thinks 2027 could be a big year
  • AI is already helping researchers do their jobs
  • What's perplexity got to do with all this?
  • OpenAI wants some ground rules before AI gets smarter
  • So, could AI really start improving AI by 2027?

Why OpenAI thinks 2027 could be a big year

Pachocki's prediction starts with an interesting discovery inside OpenAI's research lab.

Advertisement

For more than a year, researchers tested AI models on difficult mathematical problems. Then they introduced a model with a log-perplexity score of around 0.76, and the results surprised them.

According to Pachocki, the model began producing mathematical solutions to problems researchers had thought about for years. Some discoveries even arrived one after another in an internal Slack conversation.

Now, Pachocki thinks something similar could happen in pretraining, the process where AI models learn from enormous amounts of data before they're fine-tuned for specific tasks.

Imagine researchers asking an AI model to find a better way to train another model. Instead of exploring every possible approach, they could use AI-generated ideas as starting points for experiments.

A successful discovery could help researchers build more capable models, which might eventually contribute to further research.

Pachocki believes breakthroughs in this area could arrive as early as 2027.

Of course, solving math problems and improving AI training methods are two different challenges. OpenAI's mathematical discoveries also need independent verification, and there's no guarantee similar results will happen in pretraining.

Advertisement

But the idea becomes more interesting when you look at what AI researchers are already accomplishing.

AI is already helping researchers do their jobs

OpenAI's November 18 research report gives us a better idea of how far AI research assistants have come.

In March 2026, OpenAI agents could complete an estimated 23% of research tasks that normally took humans two to four hours. By October, that number had climbed to 46%.

For longer assignments requiring four to eight hours, success rates improved from 13% to 35%.

Some research tasks were easier for AI than others. Agents completed 79% of assignments related to monitoring training runs, but only 25% of tasks involving code for inference and serving systems.

OpenAI also shared how Codex contributed to research on its GPT-6.2 Astra model. In one example, the coding agent suggested a change that helped a researcher's pretraining idea work more effectively.

Researchers still have to test those suggestions and decide which ones deserve further attention.

Advertisement

OpenAI also says most of its recent progress in pretraining comes from years of research and computing investments. AI automation has contributed a smaller share.

So, AI is already helping scientists with some difficult research tasks. Whether it can consistently discover better training methods is still an open question.

What's perplexity got to do with all this?

Pachocki also wants AI companies to pay closer attention to a measurement called perplexity.

The name sounds complicated, but the basic idea is fairly simple.

When an AI model reads text or code, it predicts what comes next. Perplexity measures how well it makes those predictions. Lower scores generally mean the model is better at predicting the next piece of information.

OpenAI reports a related measurement called log-perplexity, or cross-entropy loss.

According to Pachocki, GPT-3.5 scored approximately 0.99 on OpenAI's current evaluation dataset, while GPT-4 reached around 0.91. Newer models have scored below 0.8.

OpenAI believes improvements in this measurement have accompanied the emergence of new mathematical and cybersecurity capabilities.

Advertisement

Pachocki wants researchers to use perplexity to track AI progress, especially as models can solve increasingly difficult problems.

There are limitations, though.

Different AI companies use different datasets, which makes direct comparisons difficult. Perplexity also doesn't capture every improvement in AI capabilities, particularly when models become better at reasoning through problems after training.

Still, Pachocki believes the measurement could help researchers identify when AI models are approaching more advanced capabilities.

OpenAI wants some ground rules before AI gets smarter

There's another part of Pachocki's proposal that deserves attention.

He wants AI developers to agree on measurable limits for future models and set monitoring requirements before moving beyond those limits.

The concern is that AI-assisted research could accelerate model development faster than scientists can understand what those models can do.

As Reuters reported, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has endorsed the idea of common industry limits.

Companies would need to agree on the measurements and determine which monitoring capabilities should be in place before development continues past each threshold.

Advertisement

For now, it's a proposal. The industry hasn't adopted binding limits based on Pachocki's recommendations.

So, could AI really start improving AI by 2027?

There's reason to pay attention to Pachocki's prediction, but the evidence doesn't establish a major breakthrough will happen next year.

OpenAI has already shown that agents can contribute to research tasks. Its mathematical experiments also suggest that some models can generate ideas that surprise experienced scientists.

The next big test is whether AI can consistently discover new training methods that work across different experiments.

If researchers can demonstrate that, the consequences could be exciting. Better training methods could eventually produce more capable scientific research assistants and coding agents. Researchers might also spend less time testing unsuccessful approaches.

But those benefits depend on AI-generated ideas producing reliable improvements that humans can verify. For now, 2027 remains Pachocki's prediction rather than an established milestone.

Advertisement

The development to watch is whether researchers can demonstrate an AI-generated training breakthrough that measurably improves future models. If that happens, we'll have much better evidence that AI can help scientists build the next generation of AI.

Marianne Sison

She helps businesses identify the right tools and apply best practices to streamline workflows and improve project performance. items.title: Euclid’s newest release unveils a cosmic treasure trove
items.summary: Back on July 1, 2023, ESA’s Euclid space telescope launched . This Falcon 9 rocket launch from July 1, 2023, carried the ESA’s Euclid mission into space. The Euclid space telescope, after deployment, commissioning, and calibration, has begun mapping out the Universe, and will…
items.author: Ethan Siegel
items.contentHtml:
Back on July 1, 2023, ESA’s Euclid space telescope launched.

This wide-field observatory is currently imaging and mapping out huge, 3D volumes of the Universe.

Alongside SPHEREx, Roman, and the ground-based Vera Rubin Observatory, Euclid heralds a cosmological revolution.

Its two main science goals are to probe dark energy’s and dark matter’s properties.

It accomplishes this by mapping out enormous numbers of galaxies across 14,000 degrees of sky.

Galaxy clustering information, in 3D space, reveals how likely galaxies are to be separated by specific distances.

A key clustering distance scale — the acoustic scale — reveals dark matter’s properties.

Complementarily, weak lensing — apparent shape distortion by foreground masses — reveals how cosmic structure grows.

Via the growth of this structure, we can probe dark energy’s nature.

Euclid, covering 14,000 square degrees cumulatively, also yields a broad range of astronomical phenomena.

Spectroscopic capabilities pin down the redshifts of distant galaxies.

Strong lenses magnify background objects, particularly within rich galaxy clusters.

Some 15,000 galaxy-galaxy strong lens candidates also appear.

Superclusters abound: containing dozens of individual galaxy clusters apiece.

Rare objects, like ring galaxies, abundantly appear.

Additionally, novel, rare, faint features appear even in well-studied galaxies.

An ongoing website, EPOD, highlights Euclid’s picture of the day.

Mostly Mute Monday tells an astronomical story in images, visuals, and no more than 200 words.

items.title: Copper prices are down. That might be a bad sign
items.summary: Wojtek Radwanski/Getty Images The copper market is in disarray, and the penny was officially removed from production on Friday. Coincidence? Actually, yes. Copper’s recent downturn has more than numismatists worried, as analysts believe it signals that the job market…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
The copper market is in disarray, and the penny was officially removed from production on Friday. Coincidence? Actually, yes. Copper’s recent downturn has more than numismatists worried, as analysts believe it signals that the job market, manufacturing, and the S&P 500 may be headed for declines.

“Flashing a death cross”

That’s not a reference to gang activity in GTA VI. A death cross is a technical pattern in finance trends that can be “a warning sign for economic growth,” as Renaissance Macro put it. Currently, the Bloomberg Industrials Metal Index, which is 40% copper, is flashing one.

Since copper is used in home construction, auto manufacturing, and data center buildouts, that’s not a great sign:

  • “When people build, buy, and invest, the order for copper is among the first to be placed. When they stop, it is among the first to be canceled,” economist Henrik Zeberg recently wrote on Substack.
  • He also said that a poor job market can correlate with a weak copper market because “a household that worries about its job does not buy a car or a house.”

On Friday, copper cost about $5.48 a pound, down from $6.89 in September.

Another driver of the falling prices, however, may be the (fading) spectre of new tariffs. There is currently no levy on raw copper being imported into the US. But President Trump’s repeated threats of enacting one since retaking office led companies to stockpile the metal stateside over the past two years:

  • The recent blue wave, widely interpreted as a rebuke of Trump’s economic policies, along with the pressure Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces over his role in the Nvidia–Megaspeed scandal, has industry watchers betting the raw copper tariff won’t come to pass after all, contributing to lower prices.

No better than bullion: Gold prices are also down, and the AI stock sell-off is partly to blame. Not every investor is selling out at a profit—some are cutting their losses, and when they do, Fast Company said, they tend to liquidate assets like gold to cover them.—HVL

items.title: Maldon Salt accused of flaky behavior
items.summary: Philip Kinsey/Adobe Stock Maldon Salt is in a bit of a pinch. The artisanal British brand—beloved by chefs everywhere for its fancy, flaky sea salts—has been peppered with questions since The Observer claims to have discovered that the salt may not be as authentic as its…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Maldon Salt is in a bit of a pinch. The artisanal British brand—beloved by chefs everywhere for its fancy, flaky sea salts—has been peppered with questions since The Observer claims to have discovered that the salt may not be as authentic as its reputation suggests.

What happened: On its website, Maldon claims it’s been harvesting its famous sea salt flakes by hand in the UK since 1882, but The Observer…observed trucks full of imported German rock salt arriving at the company’s production facility, prompting an explanation from Maldon. The company defended its process, but acknowledged it could have been more up-front about how the German rock salt factors into things.

Deepflake technology?

Maldon explained that it takes local seawater, filters it through the rock salt to create a brine, lets it evaporate, then hand-harvests the flakes left behind. And since the imported salt is from an ancient sea, it’s still technically 100% sea salt, even if the sea dried up in prehistoric times.

Salt burn: Still, some customers weren’t thrilled to hear that they’ve been stunting on their friends with dried-rock-salt brine this whole time. And if people start viewing Maldon as less than premium, it could hurt their bottom line. According to the New York Times:

  • One 8.5-ounce box of Maldon Sea Salt Flakes costs about $13.
  • From March 2024 to March 2025, Maldon made $51 million in global revenue.

Big picture: Neither British nor US regulators have a hard-and-fast definition of sea salt.—BC

items.title: Thinking Machines Built an AI That Thinks in Loops. Why Does It Need Less Memory?
items.summary: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini uses an unusual trick to improve AI reasoning: repeating calculations through the same neural-network layers. Early tests suggest the approach could make smaller models more capable.
items.author: Marianne Sison
items.contentHtml:
SHARE
Add The Neuron as a preferred source

Thinking Machines Built an AI That Thinks in Loops. Why Does It Need Less Memory?

Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini uses an unusual trick to improve AI reasoning: repeating calculations through the same neural-network layers. Early tests suggest the approach could make smaller models more capable.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 23, 2026
· 5 minute read

Someone at Thinking Machines Lab got an AI to build a playable flight simulator while sitting on an airplane. The impressive part? The model was running entirely on a MacBook, with no internet connection.

The AI behind the demo is called Inkling 2 Mini, and it has a rather unusual way of solving problems. It runs information through the same parts of its neural network multiple times, almost like someone who goes over a difficult question before answering.

The result is an AI model that takes up about 20 GB of storage and delivers surprisingly competitive reasoning performance.

It's an interesting development at a time when AI companies are spending billions to build increasingly powerful systems. Thinking Machines is exploring another possibility: What happens when you give a smaller model more opportunities to work through a problem?

  • How does an AI think in loops?
  • Why does it need so little memory?
  • Can it compete with bigger models?
  • There's one thing researchers still want to understand
  • Could this change the future of local AI?

How does an AI think in loops?

Advertisement

Here's the easiest way to understand it.

Most AI models process information through a series of neural-network layers. Each layer does some computation and passes the result to the next one until the model produces an answer.

Inkling 2 Mini follows a slightly different routine. It has 24 layers, but the middle 12 layers repeat their calculations three times for every token, which is a small piece of text.

Imagine working through a tricky math problem. You make an initial attempt, review your calculations, and use what you've learned to improve your answer. Inkling 2 Mini follows a somewhat similar process, except everything happens through neural-network computations.

The model effectively performs 48-layer operations while storing the weights for only 24 layers.

According to Thinking Machines, repeating the middle layers worked better than repeating the final layers in 27 out of 28 evaluations.

So the model gets additional computation from the same set of parameters. It has more opportunities to process information before producing its next token.

Advertisement

Why does it need so little memory?

Here's where the design gets interesting.

AI models typically need more memory as their parameter counts grow. Parameters are the numerical values a model learns during training, and they occupy memory when the model runs.

Inkling 2 Mini contains 26.4 billion parameters, but it doesn't activate every parameter whenever it processes a token.

Instead, it uses a technique called mixture of experts. Think of it as having several specialists available and calling on only the ones needed for a particular task.

Thinking Machines also removed two-thirds of the model's experts during training, then trained the remaining ones to recover much of the lost performance.

The looping design helps, too. Since the model reuses its middle layers, it can repeat calculations without needing separate sets of weights for every pass.

Finally, the company uses a method called quantization, which stores most of the model's weights in a smaller numerical format.

Advertisement

All of this brings the model's footprint down to approximately 20 GB.

There's one detail worth clarifying: 20 GB refers to the model itself. The official model card recommends at least 32 GB of memory for supported Apple Silicon devices.

For its airplane demo, Thinking Machines used a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip and 48 GB of memory. The model reportedly built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes, completely offline.

That's a pretty memorable way to demonstrate local AI.

Can it compete with bigger models?

An unusual architecture is interesting, but the real test is whether the model can solve difficult problems.

Thinking Machines reported a score of 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, a coding benchmark, and 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2.

The independent results from Artificial Analysis are particularly interesting.

Its evaluation found that Inkling 2 Mini matched Qwen3.8-27B on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index despite using roughly five times fewer active parameters.

Advertisement

It also used approximately 2.8 times less compute under the evaluation's measurement method.

There's a cost difference, too. Artificial Analysis reported an average of $0.59 per benchmark task for Inkling 2 Mini, compared with $3.53 for Qwen3.8-27B.

Of course, those results come from specific benchmarks. They don't mean Inkling 2 Mini is automatically better at every task.

Thinking Machines acknowledged that the model struggles with some complex instructions and difficult reasoning problems.

There's also only so much knowledge a model can learn from its training. Running the same layers repeatedly won't magically give it information that it never learned.

Still, the results suggest repeated computation can help a relatively small model compete with systems that activate substantially more parameters.

Advertisement

There's one thing researchers still want to understand

Something interesting happens when an AI performs more of its reasoning internally.

It can sometimes reach an answer while producing fewer written reasoning steps.

Thinking Machines observed this behavior in experiments with a research version of Inkling. Additional loops improved some results while shortening the visible reasoning traces.

That's worth investigating because the text an AI produces doesn't necessarily reveal everything happening inside its neural network.

Researchers at Goodfire have started examining how information changes as it passes through Inkling's repeated layers.

Their work could help researchers understand what the model learns during successive passes, especially when it solves problems with relatively little visible explanation.

For now, the findings are early. There's plenty left to learn about how repeated internal computation affects an AI's behavior.

Advertisement

Could this change the future of local AI?

One of the most interesting possibilities is what models like Inkling 2 Mini could mean for people who want to run AI on their own computers.

Local AI already has some obvious advantages. It can work offline, and users can keep certain information on their own devices instead of sending it to a cloud service.

But hardware requirements remain a challenge, especially for models capable of more demanding reasoning tasks.

Inkling 2 Mini offers another approach to that problem. Developers can give a model more computation while reusing the same weights, which limits how much memory the model requires.

For someone building an offline coding assistant or an AI tool that works with local documents, that could eventually open up more options.

The model's open weights and Apache 2.0 license also give developers room to experiment with the architecture.

Of course, Inkling 2 Mini still needs a fairly capable computer, and the looping technique has its own computational costs.

Advertisement

But its early results raise an interesting question about where AI development goes next.

We've spent years watching companies make AI models bigger. Thinking Machines is exploring how much more performance developers can get from the parameters they already have.

And if the technique continues to improve, the next impressive AI model might need considerably less hardware than we'd expect.

Marianne Sison

She helps businesses identify the right tools and apply best practices to streamline workflows and improve project performance. items.summary: Architect Labs says AI agents designed Frostbite, a CPU that delivered 4.59x better performance per watt in simulations. The agents developed a way for processing units to share tasks. Researchers still need to test those results on physical hardware.

AI Agents Designed a New CPU. Can It Really Be 4.59 Times More Efficient?

Architect Labs says AI agents designed Frostbite, a CPU that delivered 4.59x better performance per watt in simulations. The agents developed a way for processing units to share tasks. Researchers still need to test those results on physical hardware.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 23, 2026
· 5 minute read

AI agents just designed a new computer processor, and one of their cleverest ideas wasn't even requested by the human engineers.

While experimenting with different designs, the agents came up with a way for idle processing units to grab unfinished work from their neighbors. The idea could help the processor get more done while using less energy.

It's part of a new CPU called Frostbite, which Architect Labs unveiled on November 18. The company claims its AI-designed processor delivered 4.59 times better performance per watt than a conventional CPU core across 25 test workloads.

The result sounds impressive, especially considering how much of the design process the AI agents handled themselves.

There's one big question, though: Will those efficiency gains hold up when Frostbite becomes a physical chip?

How did AI agents design an entirely new CPU?

Architect Labs wanted to find out whether AI agents could develop a processor architecture rather than simply improve an existing design.

Advertisement

The researchers gave the agents computational tasks to optimize and let them investigate different ways to execute those tasks efficiently.

After reviewing existing research, the agents settled on an approach called interaction nets, a computational model that dates back to 1990.

Here's the basic idea. Most traditional CPUs execute instructions in a sequence, although modern processors can handle multiple instructions simultaneously. Interaction nets represent computations as connected nodes, so calculations that don't depend on one another can happen at the same time.

Frostbite uses this concept to distribute work across smaller processing units.

The agents also helped develop the processor's instruction set, compiler, and circuit design. To check their work, Architect Labs used a specification language called ASL, connected to the Lean theorem prover, which can mathematically verify certain properties of a design.

The team also created Arcmodel, a software representation of the processor that allowed agents to test ideas before running more expensive circuit simulations.

Advertisement

The agents went through four rounds of exploration and a final evaluation of design changes. They tested 58 ideas and kept 37 that showed enough promise to become part of the design.

And during those experiments, something interesting happened.

The AI came up with a feature nobody asked for

Frostbite divides processing work among small units called tiles.

Each tile handles its own calculations, but the amount of available work can change as a program runs. Some tiles might finish early while their neighbors still have plenty to do.

The agents developed a way to handle this automatically.

When one tile runs out of tasks, it can borrow work from another tile nearby. If there's no work available, the idle tile can become inactive to conserve power.

Think of a team where someone finishes their assignment early and helps a coworker who still has a full plate. The team gets through its workload faster because fewer people are sitting idle.

Frostbite applies a similar idea inside the processor.

According to Architect Labs, the agents developed this particular hardware implementation even though the human researchers had never explicitly requested it.

Advertisement

The feature is interesting because it shows how autonomous experimentation can produce design decisions that engineers didn't anticipate.

Of course, the underlying concept of work stealing already exists in computer science. What's unusual here is how the agents arrived at their own hardware implementation during the design process.

So, is Frostbite really 4.59 times more efficient?

Here's where the results need a little context.

Architect Labs compared a four-tile Frostbite processor against a similarly sized conventional CPU core. According to Tom's Hardware, the comparison processor was a dual-issue, in-order design, meaning it could issue two instructions at once but followed a relatively fixed execution order.

The results were encouraging:

  • 4.59x better performance per watt across all 25 workloads.
  • 6.02x better efficiency on 10 workloads used to optimize the design.
  • 3.83x better efficiency on 15 workloads excluded from optimization.
  • 8.77x better performance per unit of chip area.

These numbers are geometric averages, so the improvement varied depending on the workload.

Advertisement

Architect Labs also hasn't identified the comparison processor, citing legal reasons. As XenoSpectrum's analysis explains, the results don't mean Frostbite will run every application 4.59 times faster.

More importantly, these numbers come from pre-silicon evaluations. The processor hasn't been manufactured yet.

Frostbite targets a 7-nanometer manufacturing process and reached 500 MHz during its final physical design evaluation, but researchers still need actual hardware measurements to confirm its efficiency.

What happens before Frostbite becomes a real chip?

Designing a processor is one challenge. Getting it to perform as expected once it's manufactured is another.

Architect Labs still needs to demonstrate how Frostbite handles real applications and whether its simulated power savings translate into measurable improvements on physical hardware.

The researchers also plan to compare it with more advanced processors using established benchmark suites such as SPEC and PARSEC.

Those comparisons should give us a better idea of how Frostbite performs against modern CPUs, especially processors that can execute instructions out of order or run multiple cores simultaneously.

Advertisement

Then there's the software issue.

Frostbite uses a new instruction set and programming model, which means existing applications would need compatible tools to run on it. The company plans to develop a preliminary operating system and provide an FPGA-hosted environment where developers can experiment with the architecture.

Architect Labs also intends to release Frostbite's hardware description and instruction set so other researchers can examine the design.

The company has already experimented with AI-driven chip development. As The Neuron previously covered, its previous Redwood project used AI to create an inference accelerator that operated on reprogrammable hardware in less than two weeks.

Frostbite takes the idea into general-purpose computing, where processors must handle a much wider variety of tasks.

And that's what makes this experiment interesting.

If the results hold up, AI agents could help engineers explore processor designs that might otherwise take considerable time and resources to investigate. More architectural experiments could mean more opportunities to find ways to improve energy efficiency.

Advertisement

For now, Frostbite gives us an early look at what AI agents can contribute to computer architecture. The next challenge is finding out whether their clever ideas work just as well on actual silicon.

Everything That Happened in AI Today (Monday, November 23, 2026)

AI agents reportedly designed a new CPU architecture; an Anthropic researcher says Claude helped produce a math proof; Trump and Xi discussed military AI safeguards; OpenAI proposed a common AI progress metric; and Meta revisited its climate deadline.

Written By
Marianne Sison
Nov 23, 2026
· 7 minute read

AI agents have designed a CPU that reportedly uses far less power. There is one rather important detail: nobody has actually manufactured the chip yet.

Welcome, humans!

The weekend brought a few curious developments in AI research. A new coding model can run on a laptop, and scientists are exploring whether AI can choose promising drug candidates. Then there's a startup that gave AI agents a bigger assignment: design a computer processor from scratch. The machines are officially applying for hardware jobs.

Meanwhile, SpaceX's enormous data-center plans have prompted questions about electricity costs, and researchers are debating how to measure the capabilities of newer AI models. We'll start with that processor design and the evidence behind its eye-catching efficiency claim. Let's get into it.

🆕 NEW From The Neuron

  • Our Riemann hypothesis explainer examines the proposed Claude-assisted proof, what the computer checks have established, and why mathematicians are still reviewing the claim.
  • Our Gemini 4 Neon comparison explains its coding performance against Claude Code and how model settings change the cost of a task.
  • Our Nvidia and Inception story looks at the opportunity behind fast diffusion-based models amid acquisition reports.
Advertisement

Around the Horn — Monday, November 23, 2026

AI agents designed an entirely new CPU, according to startup Architect Labs. The Frostbite design describes a general-purpose processor with a new instruction set and a different way of breaking programs into pieces that can run in parallel. Rather than make a conventional CPU discover which steps can happen simultaneously, the architecture represents a program as connected operations that can be processed independently.

In simulated tests across 25 workloads, Architect Labs reported 4.59 times the performance per watt of a similarly sized conventional in-order CPU. The comparison dropped to 3.83 times on the 15 workloads that received no AI-specific tuning. Both numbers come from a pre-silicon 7-nanometer design. The startup has not fabricated a physical processor, and it has not publicly named the comparison CPU.

Those qualifications matter because simulation can show whether a design is promising, while a manufactured chip would test real-world power consumption and performance. The claim points to a novel role for AI agents in hardware research: they could help investigate different computing architectures rather than merely tune existing chip layouts. The next test is independent examination of the design, followed by actual silicon.

Advertisement

🏆 TOP 5 NEWS (Around the Horn)

  • Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped solve a famous math mystery. Levent Alpöge published a computer-checkable proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. Independent mathematicians have compiled the Lean code, but they are still examining whether the formal statement proves the intended claim; a separate, human-written proposed proof has emerged too. Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang called it a turning point for AI-assisted intellectual work. The theorem has not been formally accepted.
  • Trump and Xi discuss keeping humans in military AI decisions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the leaders agreed to retain human involvement in major military decisions that use AI. Semafor reports additional interest in joint AI safeguards even as Washington restricts advanced chip exports. The remarks describe political commitments; implementation requirements have yet to be established.
  • SpaceX faces a power-bill question over $74 billion in AI facilities. The proposed Texas and Arizona computing campuses include a roughly 6-gigawatt Arizona electricity demand at full build-out. Residents and officials want evidence that grid expansion and related costs will fall on the developer rather than local ratepayers.
  • OpenAI proposes a shared way to measure AI progress. Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published the company's internal perplexity measurements and argued that next-token prediction performance can provide a common indicator of progress across labs. The proposal aims to improve comparisons and inform AI safety discussions, though prediction performance alone cannot establish how a model behaves on every real-world task.
  • Meta rethinks its 2030 climate timetable. Meta said it is re-evaluating its net-zero milestones as AI infrastructure expands. Its reported total emissions increased from 15.6 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million in 2025, roughly a 40% rise.
Advertisement

Honorable Mentions

  • AI progress is getting harder to test. METR warned that AI research capabilities are advancing quickly, while familiar benchmarks may exaggerate real-world autonomy, and the current evidence cannot exclude a period of rapid acceleration.
  • Researchers traced leaks through AI hosting services. An investigation with nearly two million traceable prompts found cases of stolen or mishandled secrets; OpenRouter subsequently removed three providers and stripped 125 endpoints of zero-data-retention eligibility. Researchers said at least three providers had been compromised.
  • OpenAI requires model-access intermediaries to obtain approval. OpenAI tightened rules for routers and gateways that resell access to its models, giving the company greater control over third-party distribution. The rule took effect November 20.
  • AI server costs can change after purchase agreements. Suppliers including Dell and HPE sought price increases of up to 45% months after deals were struck.
  • Nothing's upcoming AI device: Nothing teased a screenless AI-native device for a December 8 unveiling. The design has appeared in social photos; its exact capabilities remain undisclosed.
Advertisement

🍪 TOP TREATS TO TRY

  • Gemini GIF generation: Google now lets users create short, looping GIFs from text prompts, photos, or videos with its Omni 1.2 Flash model. Users can also choose GIF templates to make custom reaction memes.
  • OpenAI Dots reaches more users: OpenAI began limited tests on ChatGPT Plus and said the proactive agent feature was expanding to Business Standard. Dots can continue assigned tasks between conversations; Plus availability remains limited.
  • Inkling 2 Mini: Thinking Machines released an open-weights coding model that reuses its middle neural-network computations for extra reasoning. A MacBook reportedly built a playable flight simulator offline, and the model can run on supported laptops with sufficient memory.
  • LingSante-3.1-flash: Ant Ling released an open-weights medical model with 560 billion total parameters and 25 billion activated per token. It targets medical reasoning and extended clinical-style workflows; the developer's benchmark claims are not evidence of clinical safety.
  • MemT-1.0-Pro: MemOS introduced a 554-billion-parameter memory-native model built with Nvidia technology. It is designed to retain task history across interactions so agents can retrieve earlier experience instead of re-sending the full conversation every time.
  • Google Agent Compute Engine: Google described a managed execution service that isolates AI agents in small virtual machines and keeps credentials outside their workspaces. Suspended sessions can resume from checkpoints.
  • OpenAI MedChemBench: OpenAI released a medicinal-chemistry benchmark with 99 research-derived problems that test whether models understand molecular evidence and can suggest promising compounds for follow-up experiments.
  • Apple iOS 27.3 beta: Apple is testing additional Siri actions and third-party app integration alongside a redesigned Health app and Apple Watch features. General third-party Siri actions are expected later than the beta.
  • YouTube Custom Feeds: YouTube lets eligible users describe a desired feed in natural language and save it on their homepage. The October feature currently requires U.S. English and enabled search history; free users can save three feeds, and Premium users can save eight.
  • Signal screenshot protections: Signal added default restrictions to stop operating-system AI assistants from reading private chats through screenshots on supported iOS and Android setups.
  • Chainalysis Chain: Chainalysis launched an AI investigation workspace in limited preview. Investigators can ask agents to trace crypto transfers across blockchains instead of manually searching multiple transaction explorers.
  • Tiny 2.1: A developer packed a 367,000-parameter question-answering model onto a floppy disk for DOS-era 486 and Pentium computers. It needs around 540 KB of memory and can speak through the PC speaker, though its knowledge is limited.
  • A starter guide to running AI at home: GPU Partner walks readers through setting up a personal AI assistant with open models such as Inkling and Qwen and local tooling such as Unsloth. Hardware requirements and setup time depend on the chosen model.
Advertisement

🏢 Big Tech & Major Companies

  • Nvidia's succession challenge: Fortune examines the next CEO's priorities after Jensen Huang's departure, including export controls, regulatory scrutiny, and scrutiny of AI infrastructure deals.
  • Anthropic after the IPO: The Wall Street Journal profiled Dario and Daniela Amodei and their effort to keep the company's unconventional culture. The Washington Post explored Dario Amodei's efforts to persuade outside thinkers of his predictions about powerful AI and its governance.

💼 AI Productivity, Labor & Economics

  • The Fed debates an economy exposed to AI enthusiasm: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned against overtightening after technology shares weakened despite Anthropic's IPO. Investors are debating whether infrastructure spending and earnings expectations have peaked.
Advertisement

📊 Fundraising & Deals Roundup

  • Europa Fusion: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing the startup, which was founded by former AI researcher Nantas Nardelli. The team wants to use simulation-intensive research to pursue pulsed-power fusion. A funding amount was not disclosed in the cited report.

🎙️ Interviews, Panels & Podcasts

  • Jason Lemkin revisits the 20VC discussion: His SaaStr follow-up focuses on Anthropic's comparatively small headcount, whether Nvidia will remain an aggressive acquirer in 2027, and his view that Meta's Muse could displace parts of marketing automation. These are Lemkin's interpretations, rather than established forecasts.
Advertisement

Previous Around the Horn Digests

Catch up on the recent issues:

  • Thursday, November 19, 2026: Anthropic's IPO, Nvidia's China shipments, and Gemini 4 Neon.
  • Wednesday, November 18, 2026: GPT-6.2 Astra, Nvidia's open-source strategy, and AI safety tests.
  • Tuesday, November 17, 2026: California's OpenAI case, chip controls, and independent safety reviews.
  • Monday, November 16, 2026: ChatGPT Wallet, Nvidia leadership, and AI supply chains.
  • Friday, November 13, 2026: Jensen Huang's resignation, SpaceX's AI campuses, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen.
  • Thursday, November 12, 2026: Databricks' assistant, AlphaGenome 2, and AI spending concerns.
Advertisement

That's a Wrap

That covers 30 stories from 35 sources, from a simulated CPU to a chatbot on a floppy. If you reached this far, congratulations: you have probably consumed more AI hardware news than your actual hardware requested.

For the daily five-minute edition, subscribe to The Neuron. See you tomorrow.
