items.title: Who’s going to profit from Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO?
items.summary: Morning Brew Inc. Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US economy.

The company will officially price its initial public offering today, before trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow under the ticker “ANT.” The IPO will not be very ant-like: Anthropic initially set shares at $70 to $78 apiece, and at the top end of its pricing, it would raise $90.4 billion, with a valuation at $1.4 trillion. As banks closed share orders yesterday afternoon, orders were seven times the number of available shares, according to Bloomberg.

  • Anthropic’s share price could be over $80 today, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
  • That would mean a valuation as high as $1.6 trillion.

As the first major AI lab to go public, the IPO is viewed as a high-stakes stress test for both the AI industry and the entire global economy. A disappointing opening would still net investors huge gains, but it’d also add further fuel to ongoing AI skepticism.

Who’s set to gain?

For starters, the 300 or so investors who threw money at Anthropic, according to PitchBook. Some of the biggest venture capital funds are already preparing the champagne bottles: Menlo Ventures was in for $750 million in 2023. Lightspeed Venture Partners led a $3.5 billion round in 2025, and earlier this year, Sequoia, Greenoaks, and Altimeter joined private equity and corporate buddies to raise Anthropic’s largest funding round of $65 billion.

  • In the first half of this year, AI has snagged $355.9 billion from VC funds. That’s 86% of all US venture capital funding in that time frame, according to Clearstead’s analysis of Pitchbook data.
  • Because so much of AI development is concentrated in San Francisco, the city is taking in a third of all global VC dollars right now, according to PitchBook.

Who else is getting rich? An average Anthropic employee could see their equity balloon to $72 million. The company’s biggest customers, Amazon and Google, are set to own roughly 28% of Anthropic’s stock after the IPO.—MM

items.title: Jensen’s former employer reports stellar earnings
items.summary: Cheng Xin/Getty Images Nvidia reported earnings yesterday, but much bigger than its revenue doubling in 12 months was the elephant in the room. The better-than-expected Q3 report card dropped days after Jensen Huang became Nvidia’s ex-CEO amid revelations about his romantic…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Nvidia reported earnings yesterday, but much bigger than its revenue doubling in 12 months was the elephant in the room. The better-than-expected Q3 report card dropped days after Jensen Huang became Nvidia’s ex-CEO amid revelations about his romantic relationships with a suspected Chinese spy, as well as two employees.

Financially, things look great. Revenue rose 20% from the previous quarter, and the company predicted it will grow 12% in Q4. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company is boosting its 2028 growth outlook from 70% to 75%, giving investors hope that the chipmaker could persevere post-Jensanity. Nvidia shares rose in after-hours trading.

But things will be different:

  • Nvidia will stop selling certain chips to China, signifying a pivot away from Huang’s push to promote ties to the country.
  • Kress said Nvidia will be “disciplined and selective” about supporting other AI companies, a sign it might retreat from its role as a financial backstop to the industry.

Jensen spoke out. In his first public statement since the ouster, Huang said earlier in the day that he’d be “honored” to return as CEO. But board chair Harvey Jones reiterated on the earnings call that that’s not being considered.

We’ll hear from him again: Huang will testify to Congress about Nvidia’s compliance with chip export controls on Dec. 1.—SK

items.title: Kalshi bets on Martha Stewart to clean up its image
items.summary: Kalshi Prediction markets are plagued by a reputation for being susceptible to insider trading. That’s why Kalshi enlisted Martha Stewart to star in a new ad warning potential customers about the consequences of rigging markets and the platform’s new safeguards against it. The…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Prediction markets are plagued by a reputation for being susceptible to insider trading. That’s why Kalshi enlisted Martha Stewart to star in a new ad warning potential customers about the consequences of rigging markets and the platform’s new safeguards against it.

The 90-second spot features Stewart—who was never convicted of insider trading but was found guilty of lying to investigators in a trading scandal—in a replica of the kitchen from her 1990s TV show preparing a pie but leaving out the ingredient of confidential information (it’s not the best metaphor).

Kalshi also announced it would follow the recommendation of an integrity committee to provide more tailored surveillance around markets depending on their risk profile. The company said that grouping marketswith similar insider trading risks together will “reduce false positives” and “focus review on higher-risk activity.”

Hours after the marketing blitz began, The Wall Street Journal reported that Kalshi is halting trading on markets that allow users to put money down on what words President Trump will say on a given date, after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission ordered it to do so on Friday. The CFTC said it was due to the ease with which these markets could be influenced. In August, a White House teleprompter operator settled an insider trading case with federal regulators.—DL

items.title: Reading is Like Love
items.summary: Welcome to The Unsolicited Advice Reading Group. This month we are reading Anne Carson’s book Eros The Bittersweet . Our schedule will be as follows: Saturday 7th November - Up to “Alphabetic Edge” Saturday 14th November - Up to “Folded Meanings” ( sorry this is so late…
items.author: Joseph Folley
items.contentHtml:
Welcome to The Unsolicited Advice Reading Group. This month we are reading Anne Carson’s book Eros The Bittersweet. Our schedule will be as follows:

Saturday 7th November - Up to “Alphabetic Edge”

Saturday 14th November - Up to “Folded Meanings” (sorry this is so late, travelling has been pretty intense and I haven’t had much time to write)

Saturday 21st November - Up to “Cicadas”

Saturday 28th November - Up to the end

Saturday 5th December - Live call for paid subscribers (6PM UK time)

If you would like to read exclusive articles and get access to our live calls, consider becoming a paid subscriber :)

Some of the chapters we’ve read this week continued on the direct theme of romantic eros and its association with related concepts of lack or distance, but since we already talked about that last week, I want to instead focus on the way that Carson takes some of the ideas she developed in a specifically romantic context, and applies them to other dynamics or activities. It would be an exaggeration to say that Carson ends up treating eros as something like a fundamental life force, but it’s not too much of one.

This theme of the book was present even at the preface, where Carson opened by writing about a philosopher in the Kafka short story “The Top”. This philosopher devotes much of his time to a seemingly meaningless pursuit - catching spinning tops while they are mid-spin, with the idea that if he could just understand it in sufficient detail, he could understand the universe itself. Of course, his pursuits fail, and each time he catches one he does not find the ultimate answers he seeks. This, however, does not prevent him from trying again the next time he sees a top mid-spin. Carson has this to say about it:

“The story is about the delight we take in metaphor. A meaning spins, remains upright on an axis of normalcy aligned with the conventions of connotation and denotation, and yet: to spin is not normal, and to dissemble normal uprightness by means of this fantastic motion is impertinent, What is the relation of impertinence to the hope of understanding? To delight?”

She makes this observation even before she talks about love and “why we love to fall in love”. The story about the philosopher is about discovery, then about metaphor and expression, and only then does Carson make it about love.

The chapter called Symbolon begins with Carson reflecting on the idea of inquiry. She points out that Socrates used erotic metaphors in his ideas about inquiry and knowledge, and that Aristotle characterised humanity as having a strange, and seemingly innate, desire to discover things. The reason inquiry resembles romantic eros, in Carson’s view, is that they share the same bittersweetness. The lover seeks to meld with their beloved, yet also keep them at a distance, and the inquirer seeks to discover, but if knowledge is achieved, then that is one less thing to discover, and so the acquiring of knowledge also comes tinged with disappointment.

Last week we talked about the Marquis de Sade as a deeply unerotic figure, because he has transgressed all distance between his own will and the wills of the people he desires (I am going to say “desires” because it feels strange to say “loves” in such a context). With no distance left to traverse, there is nothing through which eros can arise. Carson’s comments here imply a similar thing with regard to inquiry and omniscience.

We might think that the object of inquiry is to know more, and of course at a first-order level, it is. But at a second-order level, it is the wish to discover, and this joy in the act of discovery implies that the inquirer currently lacks some important piece of knowledge. In just the same way that the lover desires both their beloved and the distance between them, the inquirer desires knowledge, but in an important sense they also desire their ignorance. Under this picture, omniscience is something outright ugly. If an inquirer were to wake up omniscient, then they would be robbed of the very activity they wish to prolong. An analogy with sport might be helpful. If I were a genie, and I told a champion boxer that from this moment on, not only would they win every match they undertook, but they would do so with ease, that they would never have to train or to think about their sport again, but would beat every opponent as easily as they would swat a fly, they might first be elated, but I don’t think it would take long for them to fall into a pretty depressed state. In sporting settings, we have no problem recognising that it is the continued activity of the sport that most sportspeople desire, rather than simply to win. I think this is one reason why winning at any cost by taking advantage of an unfair opportunity is considered “poor sportsmanship”. Not only is it bad manners, it is acting directly against the meta-aim of the sporting event, which is to have the best example of the activity possible.

I like applying this framework to inquiry because it recontextualises the very concept of ignorance. Here ignorance remains undesirable at one level, in the sense that it is something the inquirer overcomes, but it becomes desirable at another, because the thing being valued is the activity of overcoming ignorance, rather than the state of having knowledge (there are some clear parallels here with Bernarrd Reginster’s analysis of the will to power, but I won’t go into them in this post). Since we are all unavoidably ignorant, this revaluing of ignorance as a necessary part of something we value (discovery) is helpful. Ideally, I would like it to encourage us to be less ashamed of our ignorance, and in some cases actively envy people who know a bit less than us about a topic. When I was at university, I started to sing in choirs, and one night I was chatting with someone who was (and indeed is) a far more experienced musician and singer than me. After a few glasses of wine, he talked about the first time he truly felt like he “melded” with a choir during a performance, and described it as totally magical. The discovery of that new feeling was highly meaningful to him, and it relied on it being a new experience, and thus on his prior ignorance. What he envied was me having that for the first time. In that context, my ignorance was desired. This gets us out of the long-induced habit of conceiving of “not-knowing” as shameful, which is good news, considering even the most erudite octogenarians among us are ignorant of far more than they know. For Carson, to be omniscient is a curse.

Carson applies a similar structure to ideas about narrative and literary meaning. Her observations here are peppered over a few chapters, expanding outwards from the level of the sentence to the level of narrative itself.

Carson first applies this erotic structure to the metaphor. Metaphors are completely ubiquitous in our speech (indeed, I think the evidence shows that they are an invaluable part of how we innovate on language). But what happens when we grasp a metaphor? Carson, drawing on Aristotle, argues that we bridge the conceptual gap between two distant concepts, and bring them closer together, temporarily melding their meanings. To take a simple example, if I refer to someone as “a wolf”, then I am drawing on all the pre-existing associations someone has of a wolf, and linking them to the person I am describing, while still recognising that the statement is literally false - this person is not a wolf. As Carson puts it:

“Thus, tension of an acute and unresolvable kind informs this mental action. It demands of the mind [...] an ability to hold in equipoise two perspectives at once.”

Carson points out that there is a similarity here between the way we understand a metaphor and the way we view a beloved. When we love someone, we inevitably come to see them in a different, heightened way. Depending on who you ask this may be delusion or it may be simply appreciation, but either way our imagination causes us to view our beloved in a very different way to the rest of the world (for an extended discussion of this, I would highly recommend Troy Jollimore’s book Love’s Vision). If metaphor is to bring two or more heterogenous associative elements together to see something in a new and richer light, while maintaining their literal distance, then it wouldn’t be too misleading to say that we perceive our beloved “metaphorically”.

Having dealt with the small scale, Carson moves on to examining narrative as a whole (and specifically the novel) as an exercise in eros. In a skilled narrative, much like in a metaphor, the words on the page are viewed at multiple levels. On the surface, there are simply the literal meanings of individual words and sentences, then there might be small-scale literary devices (such as metaphors), then there are the higher-order properties like the ordering of events and the way the chapters or books are structured, and then there is the thematic realm, where we temporarily step outside the flow of the narrative and look at what the story, conceived of almost as its own person, is attempting to communicate or explore. This requires the same “stereoscopic” vision as a metaphor, but with significantly more complexity. It is also an erotic relationship, both for how it plays with the imagination of the reader, but also in how it plays with closeness and distance, absence and presence. At once the reader is encouraged to lose themselves in the details of the work, and maintain enough distance to appreciate it as a whole. The way we can develop our own idiosyncratic interpretations of rich stories only adds to this. Carson points out that Helen of Troy is not described in The Iliad, so as to let the mind of the reader fill in the blanks. The eroticism of the character is enhanced by the fact that each person can conjure up their own idea of the most beautiful woman in the world to occupy this placeholder. In a particularly rich text, a similar phenomenon occurs whereby the reader is able to pick out the particular threads which they find most compelling, and individual differences ensure that countless interpretations flourish, all of which can still be rooted in the text itself, without someone being able to cast final judgment on the absolute, capital-T-True interpretation of the work. This is sometimes seen as an indication that literature is a waste of time. Instead, it is an indication that the act of reading itself is erotic, in Carson’s sense of the term.

And on that note, there is something about the way that Carson’s book itself is written that I find both in keeping with her ideas, and interesting in its own right. So far, the chapters have an overlapping structure. Carson will introduce an idea and develop it, and then will often take one step back at the beginning of the next chapter, before introducing the next idea and development. This gives the book a kind of yearning or reaching in its structure, where rather than an idea being stated outright, Carson reaches out to grab it, then retreats, then reaches again, making a little more progress, before another small retreat, and so on. The literary structure of the book mirrors the process of a lover becoming closer with their beloved, while at the same time wishing to maintain a distance between them. It also gives the work a kind of flowering structure, where instead of stating a definition of eros at the beginning of the book, eros gradually unfurls itself chapter-by-chapter, through the exploration of various contexts and examples. I don’t know if this is deliberate or just a happy accident, but I love it when a work manages to be an example of what it is discussing. Eros the Bittersweet (at least so far) is a kind of love story between Carson and the concept she is investigating, and in that sense it manages to capture all three of the central examples of eros: romance, inquiry, and narrative, that Carson has discussed thusfar.

I am really enjoying re-reading this - there is an awful lot that I had missed! Carson covers a lot of different topics so I haven’t been able to cover them all, so I would be interested to know if different elements of her work leapt out at you.

items.title: US reacts to Nvidia scandal by curbing chip exports
items.summary: Xinhua/Getty Images Uncle Sam is limiting China’s access to AI chips after last week’s revelation that Nvidia’s now-resigned CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Yesterday, the Commerce Department took steps to close a loophole Chinese…
items.author: Sam Klebanov
items.contentHtml:
Uncle Sam is limiting China’s access to AI chips after last week’s revelation that Nvidia’s now-resigned CEO Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Yesterday, the Commerce Department took steps to close a loophole Chinese companies exploited to skirt US export controls on advanced AI chips by using data centers in nearby countries. Under the department’s new rule:

  • Chipmakers like Nvidia will be barred from supplying advanced chips to overseas data centers servicing companies in places like China and Russia.
  • There’ll be a new licensing process for exporting chips to several countries that often serve as a stopover for China-bound chips.

Huang chip diplomacy is kneecapped. The change endangers a Huang-fostered ecosystem of Asian data centers offering Chinese companies like Alibaba and ByteDance remote access to Nvidia’s AI chips. Shares of Nvidia, as well as its rivals Intel and AMD, dropped yesterday.

Two hands, one pen

The Commerce Department said its new rule was written by the Treasury Department, an unprecedented disclaimer experts say exposes a long-running rift in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking chip export controls. Both secretaries will accompany President Trump on this week’s Asia trip, where he’ll meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.

Meanwhile…Trump said he would “not mind” seeing Huang return as CEO, but Nvidia’s board is reportedly not considering his reinstatement.—SK

items.title: Amazon MGM has a new 007: Robert Pattinson
items.summary: Illustration: Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Amazon MGM Studios Finally, a story about a spy that has nothing to do with Jensen Huang. Amazon MGM announced yesterday that Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond, a casting decision that ends seven years of speculation and finally has…
items.author: Dave Lozo
items.contentHtml:
Finally, a story about a spy that has nothing to do with Jensen Huang. Amazon MGM announced yesterday that Robert Pattinson is the new James Bond, a casting decision that ends seven years of speculation and finally has the studio positioned to see a return on its heavy investment into the franchise.

  • In 2022, Amazon acquired MGM for $8.5 billion—that included a 50-50 split of the Bond rights with the Broccoli family, who had final say in creative decisions.
  • So Amazon tossed another reported $1 billion at the longtime stewards of the martini-swilling character in March 2025 to wrest away their veto power.

And now, the studiothat brought us Red One and Mercy has tapped Pattinson, the first new Bond since Daniel Craig announced in 2019 that 2021’s No Time To Die would be his final appearance after 15 years as the character. The 40-year-old Pattinson, who may consider himself the first Gen Z Bond, eclipsed rivals for the role that reportedly included Jack Lowden (Slow Horses), Josh O’Connor (Challengers), and Callum Turner (Dua Lipa’s Husband).

It’s a deviation from previous Bond casting choices under the Broccoli family, who preferred lesser-known actors that wouldn’t overshadow the character. But as Puck News theorized, a known entity like Pattinson, who has already anchored franchises as Batman and a sparkly vampire, may feel more necessary considering how much Amazon has invested.

What else is likely to change?

Since Bond made its big screen debut in 1962 with Dr. No, the official franchise has earned an inflation-adjusted $7 billion at the domestic box office. Now, imagine how much more it would have made if there was a spinoff series centered around Le Chiffre, or a Pussy Galore origin story available to stream in your home? There’s been speculation that those types of Bond-related projects could be in the offing with Amazon in possession of the IP.

In theaters when? Production timelines suggest that Pattison could make his Bond debut in 2028—and, if true, that seven-year gap between movies will be the longest in the franchise’s history.—DL

items.title: International students are ditching US colleges
items.summary: Paul Kuroda/Getty Images A growing number of young adults overseas cannot relate to the West Side Story lyric, “I like to be in America.” Amid the Trump administration’s changing visa policies and an overall jump in higher education costs, international enrollment is falling at…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
A growing number of young adults overseas cannot relate to the West Side Story lyric, “I like to be in America.” Amid the Trump administration’s changing visa policies and an overall jump in higher education costs, international enrollment is falling at US universities, according to data released yesterday.

New international student enrollment dropped 15% for fall 2026 compared to the fall 2025 semester, according to a survey of 800+ colleges by the nonprofit Institute of International Education:

  • Graduate students accounted for the bulk of the dropoff.
  • Among schools where international enrollment declined, 88% cited the visa application process as a contributing factor, while 70% noted travel restrictions, and 45% referenced degree costs.

Though some government officials argue this benefits US students, leaders in higher education say otherwise: International students tend to pay full tuition, which makes their matriculation a key revenue source for colleges and universities—one that can help subsidize financial aid and other services for domestic students.

Feeling the burn: Citing drops in international enrollment (along with a drop overall for both undergrad and graduate students), Penn State University is facing a $124 million budget gap for its next fiscal year, and the Illinois Institute of Technology said it plans to borrow $200 million from its endowment.

Zoom out: With international students contributing almost $40 billion to the US economy last school year, this fall’s enrollment dropoff is expected to cost Uncle Sam $2.4 billion, according to NAFSA, an international education association.—ML

items.contentHtml:
Claude Code + Obsidian: My family’s AI brain | Scott Farrar

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence

Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who built a shared household brain using Claude Code and Obsidian. In this episode, he shows how the system tracks appliances and warranties, compares insurance quotes, organizes family projects, and keeps household tasks moving through a shared to-do list and wall display. He also explains why persistent files work better for him than long AI chats, and how the same philosophy shapes his approach to using AI without taking the thinking away from students.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The problem with chat is not intelligence, but memory drift. Scott moved to Claude Code because it stores context in Markdown files he can inspect, correct, and reuse across sessions. His memory is no longer trapped inside an opaque conversation.

  2. Let the AI tell you what context it needs. When Scott asked Claude how to document his home, it suggested photographing every appliance. Those photos became a searchable inventory of model numbers, serial numbers, and warranty details.

  3. Unstructured input is fine when the system handles the organization. Scott gives Claude raw information and lets it maintain the underlying files. A custom linter prevents verbose agents from bloating documents such as his household to-do list.

  4. Better context helps people ask better questions. Claude compares insurance quotes with detailed information about Scott’s home, identifies potential coverage gaps, and prepares specific follow-ups. He no longer has to rely entirely on the agent selling him the policy.

  5. One master list can eliminate a house full of mental clutter. Scott and his wife captured every household task they could think of, then Claude organized them by priority, cost, and supporting information. The system now surfaces overdue work before it becomes another fire.

  6. Multiplayer household systems require practical compromises. Claude recommended GitHub to avoid file conflicts, but that added more complexity than Scott’s wife wanted. They settled on GitHub for shared scripts and Dropbox for everyday files, matching the tools to how they actually work.

  7. A household system becomes more useful when it leaves the laptop. Scott’s wall display shows upcoming trips, open tasks, recent wins, and small daily suggestions. It turns a private collection of files into something the whole family can see and use.

  8. Scott rebuilt his father’s file cabinet as an AI system. His dad saved every receipt and warranty and could explain repairs from decades ago. Claude now gives Scott that same dependable household memory, only searchable through conversation.

  9. AI should help children think, not think for them. Scott prefers tutors that ask students to explain their reasoning and work through productive struggle. He also believes some children may share unfinished ideas more comfortably with AI than with another person.

  10. Infinite patience is not always good teaching. Scott wants AI to act as a “warm demander” that encourages students without doing the work for them. When his own agent goes off track, he starts fresh or investigates its reasoning before incorrect information reaches his memory files.

How I fight token fraud as a solo founder

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Auros—The human network behind AI

In this solo episode, Claire explains how token fraud cost ChatPRD tens of thousands of dollars and consumed much of her engineering time. She walks through six forms of abuse, including farmed free trials, resold promo codes, card testing, product relays, and a custom MCP running as a 24/7 compute worker. She also shares the business and technical defenses she built, how Jev classifies suspicious activity in real time, and why she ultimately eliminated free trials.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Token fraud is a business risk most AI founders underestimate until the bill arrives. Unlike traditional SaaS abuse, every fraudulent model call costs real money. It cost Claire tens of thousands of dollars despite ChatPRD being SOC 2 compliant, regularly penetration-tested, and run by an experienced technical founder.

  2. Free trials may no longer work for AI products. Fraudsters automated account creation and used ChatPRD’s most expensive models for unrelated work. Claire ultimately removed free trials, sacrificing a valuable source of product-led growth and enterprise leads after credit-card gates and paid trials also failed.

  3. Promo codes have become a serious attack vector. Codes intended for partners were stolen, resold, and used to power other AI businesses. After discovering that roughly half of her promo codes had reached resellers, Claire stopped issuing them entirely.

  4. MCP access creates a new category of abuse. One fraudster turned ChatPRD’s custom MCP support into a compute worker that ran around the clock. Claire responded by restricting approved hosts and blocking free tunnels and infrastructure that did not appear connected to legitimate companies.

  5. Cheap decision models can classify fraud in real time. When a session crosses ChatPRD’s abuse threshold, a zero-data-retention Jev loop categorizes the activity. Confirmed fraud results in either a ban or a silent downgrade to a less expensive model.

  6. AI support agents need firm boundaries around fraud. After mass bans, ChatPRD received both clumsy appeals and polished messages written by AI. Claire equipped her support agent with fraud tools and explicit rules preventing it from restoring accounts or distributing promo codes.

  7. Blunt defenses are sometimes the most effective. Blocking traffic from certain countries using Vercel Firewall significantly reduced abuse and forced Claire to reconsider ChatPRD’s international strategy. Her new default is simple: trust must be earned rather than assumed.

  8. Token fraud is affecting companies of every size. Claire found the same people abusing ChatPRD through rotating proxies across several major AI products. She has started discussing the problem publicly and filed FBI cybercrime reports with help from Codex.

  9. If a company sells AI, it is ultimately selling compute. Founders should track dollars instead of requests, monitor model spending continuously, close every free entry point, and verify the client rather than only the account. Claire also learned that fraud disappears quickly when expensive models are no longer available to steal.

Token Fraud Is Eating AI Margins. Here’s How Claire Vo Is Fighting It: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/token-fraud-is-eating-ai-margins-here-s-how-claire-vo-is-fighting-it
↳ Detect Automated Abuse on AI Routes with Vercel BotID: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/detect-automated-abuse-ai-routes-botid
↳ Use an AI Assistant to Create Payment Fraud Rules: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/use-an-ai-assistant-to-create-payment-fraud-rules

I was a Claude hater. Fable 5.2 changed my mind.

Listen now on YouTube • • Apple Podcasts

In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Fable 5.2 to see whether Anthropic has finally built a model she enjoys using. She turns a tweet into an animated marketing video, creates assembly instructions from photos of unboxed furniture, reworks a complex ChatPRD pipeline, and builds a fully functional 3D typewriter. She also explains where Fable fits alongside Opus 5.5, why its creative work impressed her, and why she still would not trust it to design a website on its own.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Fable 5.2 turned Claire from a Claude skeptic back into a fan. She found the original Fable difficult to understand and unpleasant to use, with Opus 5 offering little improvement. Fable 5.2 feels fast, capable, creative, and dramatically easier to work with.

  2. Fable 5.2 complements Opus 5.5 rather than replacing it. Opus remains the better default for most coding and knowledge work. Fable is the model Claire would choose for greater complexity, broader scope, or tasks that demand more creativity.

  3. Its speed changes how the model feels to use. Many benchmark tasks finished in under a minute, and even a complex animation took only 16 minutes. Fable also communicates sparingly during autonomous work, surfacing only the moments that require input.

  4. Fable 5.2 made AI video feel animated instead of assembled. From one tweet and the CXO.dev brand guidelines, it created a narrated story featuring custom invader-bot sprites that walk, jump, and cheer. No other model Claire tested produced anything comparable, so the task is becoming a permanent benchmark.

  5. Its spatial reasoning solved a real-world problem every other model failed to. Claire gave Fable low-resolution photos of an unassembled piece of furniture with no instructions. It identified the parts, created a diagram, and produced the correct assembly sequence, which her household successfully followed.

  6. Fable 5.2 is unexpectedly funny. It designed a bug-fighting game around real engineering tradeoffs, then made a trailer in which finance sees the token bill and downgrades the team to a cheaper model. The humor felt intentional enough to make Claire genuinely laugh.

  7. It also holds up on serious engineering work. Fable created a sensible migration plan for ChatPRD’s messy product-intelligence pipeline and aligned closely with Claire’s own roadmap. It worked autonomously and paused at appropriate moments, though the migration is still underway.

  8. Fable needs strong direction for visual design. It follows an existing brand system well, but its unguided web and storybook designs were unattractive. Claire expects to pair it with Opus 5.5 for frontend work and use a separate image model when original visuals are needed.

  9. The 3D typewriter was Claire’s “AGI moment.” Fable built a working keyboard in one shot, then added white-out, music, weather, timers, writing prompts, and multiple immersive settings. It turned an idea Claire never imagined building into a tool she wants to use every day.

  10. Fable 5.2 is available now, with an even faster mode coming. It is launching across the Claude API, cloud platforms, Claude apps, and Claude Code. Claire plans to compare it with the other new models in a full How I AI benchmark.

items.title: Doing More vs. Doing What Matters: The Productivity Shift You Need
items.summary: This article was originally published on Substack . The Hollow Chase The day I accomplished more in 6 hours than I had in previous weeks of 40+ was the day I realized everything I knew about productivity was wrong. During my PhD, I found myself working one full-time job plus…
items.author: Lia Luzong
items.contentHtml:
This article was originally published on Substack.

The Hollow Chase

The day I accomplished more in 6 hours than I had in previous weeks of 40+ was the day I realized everything I knew about productivity was wrong.

During my PhD, I found myself working one full-time job plus five part-time gigs (bartending, TA for two classes, assistant for the HDR office, and, only in Australia, delivering the school’s tea service for longer classes) while studying full-time in order to raise $22,000 for one semester’s tuition. And I had two semesters left to go.

My schedule, unsurprisingly was compressed to breaking point. I would wake up early, work late after one or more of my jobs had finished, and weekend breaks were a myth.

The surprising part? In the mere 15-20 hours I had left for my PhD work each week, I was accomplishing twice as much as when I had 40+ hours available in the years prior.

Scarcity had created clarity.

With so little time available, I became ruthlessly focused on what would move the needle. Everything else was stripped away. There was no time for second-guessing or procrastination—only the essential remained.

Saturdays became my heavy work day. Wake up at 7am, meet my friend at the gym at 730, sit down for coffee, breakfast, and work at 9am and knock out 3-4 sessions of focused 120 minute working time, changing location (I am a notorious café hopper) to keep it fresh, and usually ending my day around 5pm with an insane amount of articles read, notes written, and next steps laid out.

In contrast, when I first started the PhD with all the time in the world to focus, I tracked my progress by counting deep work sessions—tallying each 25-minute focused block. At first, this input-focused approach helped build the focus muscle, slowly building to 90 minutes of pure, focused flow time.

But eventually, I had to ask: What was all this productivity actually producing? Sure I was putting time on the calendar, but was I moving the needle? Was I actually getting closer to producing a written thesis?

The answers were all a resounding no. And it took adding 60 hours of real job(s) to my calendar to finally do something about it.

This is the hollow chase that traps so many of us: we optimize our systems, track our metrics, implement the latest productivity hack to pursue recognition—all while avoiding the harder question of whether we're moving efficiently in the entirely wrong direction.

Now that I work in consulting, I find this focus even harder to maintain. Work, social life, identity, building my own business, and sales all blur together. The clear boundaries have disappeared, and with them, the clarity of purpose that had made those limited PhD hours so productive.

And it’s not something that can just be fixed by “WORK HARDER!” As a former athlete, and since my earliest days of soccer, I knew how to push through pain and work. I knew how to grind. I can white knuckle and throw long hours at a problem.

But hours worked can’t solve everything. It’s a good starting point, but it’s probably not enough on it’s own to get you to the finish line you need.

This struggle illuminates something essential about real productivity: it's not about doing more. It's about doing what matters.

Real vs. Shallow Productivity

Busyness as a badge of honor is bullshit.

"Being busy is a form of laziness—lazy thinking and indiscriminate action." — Tim Ferriss

There's lots of work we can do simply to make people leave us alone. Work that looks impressive but doesn't move the needle. Work that creates the appearance of productivity without the substance.

This was me early on the PhD attending workshops that had very little direct value to writing my thesis. This is everytime you open your inbox pretending to check emails in order to make it look like you’re doing something while at the office. In fact, part of why virtual work is effective is because it removed the need for this fake productivity virtue-signalling.

That's not fulfilling. That's not energizing. That's shallow, unecessary shenanigans.

Real productivity, by contrast, tries to tick as many of these boxes as possible:

  • It's aligned with our meaning and purpose

  • It helps us grow and improve

  • It allows us to reach deep levels of concentration (flow)

Sometimes you only get one. The holy trinity is when you can reach all three—what I call "Value-Aligned Productivity." These are the supercharged hours where you accomplish in 60 minutes what used to take four hours, working at the intersection of flow, purpose, and mastery.

Value-Aligned Productivity means aligning your work with your core values at a time when you do your best work, creating a virtuous cycle where your actions reinforce what matters most to you, rather than depleting your energy on tasks that feel meaningless. Having just two hours of this type of work in your week can transform your experience from good to great. Having one hour of this every day can absolutely change your life—creating momentum that carries into all aspects of your work and personal development.

This is where our values enter the equation. When I approach sitting down to write as something I have to do versus this is a practice of my value of growth, in getting better at writing and documenting my own journey in order to better serve others, my relationship with the work transforms entirely. It becomes something I look forward to as opposed to dread.

The approach, the energy, and ultimately the output are fundamentally different when the work connects to what we truly value.

Think about the last time you were so locked in on a task that time seemed to disappear. Maybe it was writing a report on a topic you found fascinating, perfecting a slide deck just so, or solving a complex problem about trying to sell to a specific client. That flow state wasn't just about pRoDuCtIvItY—it was about alignment.

The Awareness Connection

Awareness—that muscle we build through meditation, journaling, and mindful practice—is crucial to distinguishing real from shallow productivity. It gives us the "catch" for interrupting patterns that don’t serve us. We either:

  1. Notice and choose our intention before approaching a task ("Even though this is a chore I dislike, I'm going to make it as enjoyable as possible" or "I'll approach this meeting by dialing up my warmth and playfulness.")

  2. Notice what we're bringing to the table during the task and choose a reframe ("I hate this, it's pointless" becomes "This is about integrity—I said I would do this, so I must.")

One of the simplest practices is setting an intention before beginning work. "I'm going to do this as fast as possible." "I'm going to approach this with humor." "I'm going to pretend this is fun." You find what you look for, so use intention to create a nudge back toward who you wish to be and how you wish to move through the world.

Without this awareness, you'll find yourself grinding through tasks that drain your energy while wondering why you're exhausted at the end of each day.

The Flow State Checklist

Flow states serve as powerful signposts that you're engaged in Value-Aligned Productivity. Research from psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (I dare you to try and pronounce his name) shows that people in flow states are up to five times more productive than when working under normal conditions, with neuroimaging studies revealing distinctive brain activity patterns during these peak performance states.

Here's what to look out for:

Typical Work:

  • You check the clock constantly
  • Your phone becomes incredibly interesting
  • You find excuses to take breaks
  • Ideas come slowly if at all
  • You feel drained afterward
  • You dread returning to it

Flow State Work:

  • Time seems to disappear
  • You forget to check your phone
  • You have to remind yourself to eat or take breaks
  • Ideas come more easily than usual
  • You feel energized after, even if physically tired
  • You look forward to returning to it

The challenge in modern workplaces is that they're often designed to inhibit flow. Open offices, constant notifications via email, slack, teams and whatever other messaging platform is out there now, back-to-back-to-back meetings, and the expectation of immediate responses… all of this is in a deep, full-fledged conspiracy against deep work. The enemy is inside the gates. The call is coming from inside the house.

The countermeasure?

Boundaries.

The Liberation of Limits

The hardest thing about boundaries is keeping them.

It's easy to say, "I want more time for things I care about—the gym, writing, going for a walk." But that requires sacrifice. It requires trading and choosing your opportunity cost.

Because you can do and accomplish just about anything you want.

But you cannot do everything you want.

To choose to go for a walk without your phone is to choose not to respond to emails or plan your work week. And you have to be okay with paying that cost.

This is what Oliver Burkeman in his best-selling book Four Thousand Weeks: Time Management for Mortals reminds us. Because we have a limited time on this earth with an infinite list of things to do, it means we have to choose, and we have to be ok with the price of those choices. That it’s not about more work, it’s about choosing the right work more often.

For me, it was so easy, for so long, to choose my job. Long hours and a lot of mental energy were dedicated to showing up and performing well as an exceptional learning designer and strategic consultant. For me, being good at my job guaranteed respect and safety. But eventually, that ran out.

Consistently choosing more work over the right work, especially the work that involved taking care of myself, is not sustainable. And it's not actually my job's responsibility to prioritize for me.

That's my job.

If I can, with a straight face and a genuine heart, tell work that I'm doing good work and that shutting my phone off at 6pm is going to help me sustainably produce great outcomes for them, then I have an obligation to protect that time.

Work is often the first place I have clients start to set boundaries, which can sound scary. Work takes up (usually) 8 hours of your day, 5 days a week. Work adds up to a third of your life, a third of the 4000 weeks you have on this planet. But at work, unlike in personal relationships, you have a job description and a contract that makes some expectations explicit about what needs to happen for "good work."

Because if you don't protect yourself and what you need to do your best work, no one will.

As long as your requests and boundaries are couched in clarity—"Here's my role, here's what I need to do my best work, and here's what I'm doing about it"—the conversation becomes much more productive. At best, they never cared in the first place. At worst, they push back strongly, and then you have every signal you need to know you're in the wrong environment.

"Daring to set boundaries is about having the courage to love ourselves even when we risk disappointing others." — Brené Brown

Where I am still a work in progress is setting boundaries with myself to protect my important-but-not-urgent time. Writing my morning pages, time for workouts—I don't treat these as sacred as I should. I get caught in immediate feelings ("I'm tired," "I want to meet friends," "I just have 30 mins of work left"). These occasional slips might be okay sometimes, but for me, they happen far more often than they should.

There's also an anxiety cost—the price you pay for not having done them in your day yet, reaching 5pm knowing you still need to workout, write a new post, and meditate. When you knock these things out early, it gives you freedom later.

This is why ritual and consistency—doing specific activities at specific times that you don't miss—are so important. They create room that you and others can plan around.

As scary bald man Jocko Willink says, "Discipline equals freedom."

Common Objections and Realistic Solutions

When discussing these approaches to productivity, I frequently hear three main objections specific to work (but hint, hint, it applies to life in general):

  • "My job doesn't allow for this kind of flexibility." Even in highly structured environments, you often have more agency than you realize. Start with small boundaries—like taking a proper lunch break or blocking 30 minutes for deep work—before attempting larger changes. Research shows that even micro-breaks of 5-10 minutes can improve focus and sustainability. The key is to begin with changes so small they don't require permission, then gradually expand your autonomy.

  • "I can't afford to work less in my competitive industry." This approach isn't about working less—it's about working differently. You have to be doing the work that only you can be doing. Your work, your team, your organization does not benefit from the time you spend on low-level tasks. We may not be able to cut out admin tasks entirely, but what and how are you working on the things that directly benefit the business? Outside of work, the same question remains. If you think you don’t have enough time, check your screen time on your phone and then re-evaluate that answer. The question isn't whether you can afford to change your approach; it's whether you can afford not to.

  • "What about urgent demands and unexpected crises?" Value-Aligned Productivity doesn't mean ignoring genuine urgencies. It means having the awareness to distinguish between true emergencies and manufactured ones. Build what author and researcher Cal Newport calls "slack" into your system—buffer time that absorbs the unexpected without derailing your most important work. When emergencies do arise, having clear values actually makes triage decisions easier because you know exactly what matters most.

The Productive Pendulum

While boundaries protect your time and energy, they're only part of the equation. The question remains: how intensely should you work within those boundaries?

This is where finding your rhythm becomes essential.

There's a tension between the David Goggins endorsed "grind" mentality and a more ‘let’s just wing it’ approach to productivity. I've found that neither extreme works perfectly.

Grind is good to have on call. You want that capacity in your engine for the days you really need it, so if this is missing, it is certifiably the place to start.

My problem, and the problem of so many high-performers I see, is learning how to shut the engine off.

Currently, I’m suffering from a little of both extremes. Between having started a new full-time job 5 months ago, just added a sales target to the role which is totally new, and launching the substack, there is a lot on my plate, and I feel like I’m doing ok on some of it, excelling at none of it.

To address this, my current approach looks like entering seasons of "push" to step up to my line of capacity, possibly a little bit over it. I’m trying to increase my capacity to work because I know I’m selling myself short in that domain. So this looks like adding an hour before work on the Substack, sometimes 2 hours after work, and usually 5-6 hours across the weekend. Between the job and this extra work, it can end up at a 60 hour work week. One week of 60 hours is doable, 6 months of that could be a superhighway to burnout.

So after these intentional push periods, I flip the focus: Where and how can I concentrate only on the highest leverage activities?

The goal becomes sustainable effort on move-the-needle tasks rather than sheer volume of hours.

It's similar to how I approach training Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. If I am always rolling at max intensity with competition-level rolls five times weekly, injury becomes inevitable. I’m 100% going to hurt myself (or be hurt by all the scary people engaging in death cuddles). And those months I would have take off injured, could have still counted if I had just dialed it back. Strategic intensity is key.

There's a rhythm and a balance to this work. Some weeks you push to your edge. Other weeks you recover. The goal isn't constant intensity, but rather a sustainable pattern and tempo that builds your capacity over time.

This approach aligns with what sports scientists call 'strategic overreaching'—temporary, planned training intensification followed by adequate recovery. Like a muscle under progressive overload, you stress your capacity, allow time to recover, and go-again, maybe just a little bit longer or harder this time. The same principles apply to cognitive work.

What's crucial here is setting a time limit for these "push" experiments. We don't want to grind indefinitely. So I might say: three weeks of doing two hours of focused work after my regular workday.

This is an experiment with a clear endpoint and evaluation: How's my energy at the end? When was I drained? What did I learn about my best times to work and how to do it sustainably?

Recognizing these patterns is half the battle. Correcting it is the other half.

Systems as Servants

After years of experimenting with productivity approaches from authors like Oliver Burkemann, Cal Newport, James Clear, Charles Duhigg, Ali Abdaal, David Allen, and others (you name it, I’ve probably read it), I've distilled a set of principles that actually serve meaning rather than just efficiency.

These are systems designed to be servants to your purpose, not masters of your time:

Single-task. Multitasking is the enemy of depth. Choose one thing and give it your full attention. This isn't just intuitive advice—it's backed by science. Heavy multitaskers pay a ‘focus tax’ for constantly switching between tasks compared to those who focused on one thing at a time. Put simply, people who believe they are 'good multitaskers' are lying to you, to me, and to themselves.

Aim for deep work and flow. Structure your environment and time to minimize distractions and maximize your chance of entering a flow state. Turn off notifications, look at a blank screen, lock the door to your office.

Know your prime time. Figure out when you work best. We can't always perfectly control our schedules, but we often have more influence than we give ourselves credit for. I'm not doing creative work in the afternoons—it has to be mornings, so I block that time out. I can meet and chat with people all day in the afternoons. This is a negotiation, not a dictatorship, but start moving your schedule toward the times and types of work that suit you best.

Have a place to track incoming tasks. Write it down. This gets things out of your head, and by seeing everything in one place, priorities often become clear.

Use the Pomodoro Technique. Start with shorter focused sessions (the standard time is 25 minutes) and increase the length as you strengthen your focus muscle.

Work around people. This isn't for everyone, but I thrive when working around others who are also working. Focusmate is a great online tool for this, where you jump on a virtual call and both work on your own thing. During my PhD, we did something called "shut up and write" that was incredibly effective. You can also ask a friend to jump on a Zoom call or meet at a café (my girlfriend and I call this "parallel play.")

Balance inputs with outputs. At the start, it's about revs and reps—how many can you do in a day/week and how do you increase those over time? Eventually, you need to shift to "What are you producing that moves the needle?" For example in sales, this means asking, "How is your activity helping to generate revenue?" This is your ultimate check against useless spinning or productivity for its own sake.

Small and consistent beats perfect and nonexistent. Some people can jump in and go all-out right away. That might work for you—I've had moments like that, usually with impending deadlines. But it's rarely sustainable. What works better is the ramp-up. With Pomodoros, my goal was always 4 hours (or 8 sessions of 25 minutes)—3 hours was not great, 5+ was exceptional. I increased session length by 5 minutes every week until eventually I was doing 90-minute blocks, consistently hitting 4-5 of those daily (6-7.5 hours of deep work). But that took about 4 months to build up to, and then I maintained that pattern for nearly 4 years.

Homework

Start by identifying one activity in your current schedule that energizes rather than depletes you. Schedule an additional 30 minutes for this activity next week, protecting this time as if it were your most important meeting. Small shifts in how you allocate your attention often trigger the biggest transformations in productivity and fulfillment.

Reimagining Productivity: The Path Forward

I still think about that period during my PhD—when financial pressure forced me to compress 40 hours of work into 15, and somehow doubled my output in the process.

The scarcity that once forced clarity can be recreated by choice. The boundaries that once felt like limitations can become the very structure that liberates your best work. What initially felt like a crisis became my greatest teacher.

These systems aren't just productivity tricks—they're unique, personal expressions of a deeper philosophy that prioritizes your alignment over sheer volume. When we step back from both the hustle culture and the work-less movement, a more nuanced approach emerges.

In the productivity conversation, most voices fall into one of two camps: the hustle-harder crowd promising that sleeping four hours a night is the secret to success, or the work-life balance advocates suggesting that the key is doing less.

Value-Aligned Productivity offers a third path—one that focuses not on how much you do, but on the alignment between what you do and who you are, and holding you to account for doing work on what you decide matters.

When I was tracking 25-minute Pomodoro sessions at the start of the PhD, I thought productivity was about showing up and putting in time. When I was juggling six jobs, I learned it was about focus and elimination. Now I understand it's about something deeper—the intersection of values, flow, and impact.

Working on this Substack has been a great example so far. It is deeply tied to my vision, mission, and values of who I wish to become in the world. It allows me to work on and improve the craft of writing. And I am able to enter deep states of flow when I set aside concentrated blocks of time - the 90-120 minutes spent writing on a Saturday morning, coffee in hand, is consistently some of my favorite and most productive time of the weekend.

For those of us who've experienced excellence in other domains—whether on the field, in academics, or early career wins—this approach offers a way to recapture that sense of purpose and mastery without sacrificing sustainability. The game has changed, but the fundamentals of meaningful achievement remain.

The path starts with awareness—noticing when you're caught in the hollow chase and choosing a different way. It continues with the courage to set boundaries, even when that means disappointing others or going against cultural norms. And it's sustained through systems that work with your natural rhythms and strengths rather than against them.

The question isn't whether you can squeeze more into each day. It's whether what you're doing matters deeply enough to warrant your limited time and precious energy.

The most productive day of your life won't be measured by tasks completed or hours logged, but by how aligned your efforts were with what truly matters to you.

What would it look like if your productivity served your purpose rather than replaced it?

What's one boundary you could set tomorrow to create space for what truly matters?

About the Author

Danny Kenny is a PhD behavioral scientist & former athlete helping high-performers bridge the gap between success and fulfillment. I transform excellence mindsets into purposeful life direction using frameworks that combine ancient wisdom with cutting-edge science.
You can find him on LinkedIn.

items.contentHtml:
Today I’m walking you through a problem that has cost me tens of thousands of dollars over the past year and eaten almost all of my engineering energy: token fraud. I’m the solo founder of ChatPRD, a bootstrapped AI platform for product managers, and fraudsters have been farming our free trials, reselling promo codes, wrapping the product in relays, and installing a custom MCP that ran as a 24/7 compute worker. I’ll walk through the six abuse patterns I’ve seen, the business and technical controls I put in place, the Jev loop that classifies fraud in real time, and why I finally killed free trials for good. If you sell AI, you sell compute.

  5. Business controls that actually slow fraud down

  6. How I use Jev to classify fraud in real time

  7. Why your AI support desk can become an attack vector

  8. What “if you sell AI, you sell compute” actually means

WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

items.title: Huang and allies eye his Nvidia C-suite comeback
items.summary: Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Over 150,000 people, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, signed petitions over the weekend signaling their steadfast support for ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by jensisting that it is jenstrumental to the US economy…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
Over 150,000 people, including Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, signed petitions over the weekend signaling their steadfast support for ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang by jensisting that it is jenstrumental to the US economy to jensure that he is returned to his old job.

Translation please? Fanboy energy aside, a superabundance of people want Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia just days after he resigned following reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, as well as two Nvidia employees:

  • On Saturday, Musk said on X that he and Huang had several high-value deals in the works and, “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”
  • The CEOs of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management, investment firms with large holdings in Nvidia, signed a letter requesting that Huang be given “a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him” and a chance to return.
  • The “Stand with Jensen” petition circulating online says it has over 160,000 signatories, including more than 8,000 current Nvidia employees (out of about 42,000 worldwide).
  • Huang himself has not commented, but the Financial Times reported yesterday that he supports his allies’ efforts to get him restored.

But obstacles remain

While it’s unprecedented for a disgraced ousted CEO to get this much immediate support for a return, it’s unclear if that’s enough for even someone with Huang’s rockstar-like following to get a top job back at a $4 trillion company amid federal investigations.

And the board did accept his resignation for…reasons. One anonymous supporter of Huang’s return to power told the Financial Times, “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense.”

At least one important figure very publicly doesn’t want him to return: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. He told Fox News yesterday that Nvidia needs “a dramatic shake-up,” saying it was “obvious” it was selling chips to Singapore shell companies, and that investigations would reveal whether this was “a low-level fail” or “up in the C-suite.”—HVL

items.title: SpaceX catches a falling Starship
items.summary: Ricardo Arduengo/Getty Images Some things are easy to catch, like a cold or an unflattering glimpse of yourself in a Target checkout camera. Some things are not, like a 171-foot-tall spacecraft plummeting back toward Earth. Nevertheless, SpaceX managed to do just that on…
items.author: Brendan Cosgrove
items.contentHtml:
Some things are easy to catch, like a cold or an unflattering glimpse of yourself in a Target checkout camera. Some things are not, like a 171-foot-tall spacecraft plummeting back toward Earth. Nevertheless, SpaceX managed to do just that on Saturday—an “epic day” that brings the company closer to a fully reusable rocket, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said on X.

A new stage

Starship launched on Friday afternoon from the southern tip of Texas, successfully entering Earth’s orbit to deploy 26 Starlink satellites. SpaceX failed to catch the rocket’s first-stage Super Heavy booster, which aborted the attempt because of a “slight underperformance of engines,” Musk said on X. SpaceX has caught Super Heavy on three previous occasions, and Musk said the failure “does not change” the timeline for fully reusable rockets.

Shipshape: The upper part of Starship made it back, though. As it approached Earth on Saturday, three of its engines kicked back on, helping it hover next to the launch tower, where two robotic “chopsticks” clamped down as smoothly as someone who just told the waiter they didn’t need a fork.

When you wish upon a Starship: Being able to quickly reuse rockets would save millions of dollars per mission and allow Starship to undertake more launches. The company said it also plans to use Starship to transport people and cargo to the moon. The spacecraft is supposed to participate in its first NASA mission, Artemis III, next year.—BC

items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
In the latest version of set-jetting to Croatia to see where they yelled “shame” at Cersei in Game of Thrones, travelers are increasingly planning their next vacations around locales from their favorite books.

According to Skyscanner’s 2026 trend report:

  • More than half of travelers (57%) had either booked a trip inspired by literature or would consider doing so.
  • Hotel searches using the site’s “library” filter surged 70% globally from the previous year, reflecting a general love for vacation reading that’s led some resorts to start their own book clubs.

Get ready with me to go to Greece: The travel company EF Ultimate Break has launched a slate of trips that take a page from BookTok, including a Percy Jackson-inspired voyage to Egypt, Greece, and Italy for $3,229. There’s also a $3,549 voyage around Switzerland for the millions of A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) fans who want to see the places that inspired their favorite fairy smut.

Tiny but mighty? The literary tourism trend has emerged despite a 40% drop-off in Americans reading for pleasure from 2003 to 2023.—ML

items.summary: Arion Press The hottest company in Silicon Valley moves very slowly in an effort to break nothing. Arion Press has been making books by hand for more than 50 years, armed with the second-largest collection of antique metal type and a whimsical machine from the 1960s. The…
items.author: Matty Merritt
items.contentHtml:
The hottest company in Silicon Valley moves very slowly in an effort to break nothing. Arion Press has been making books by hand for more than 50 years, armed with the second-largest collection of antique metal type and a whimsical machine from the 1960s.

The company publishes just three titles per year, usually ornate reprints of classics. The bespoke books, often with new illustrations and carefully crafted covers, are sent to subscribers, who pay either $3,500 or $10,000 per year depending on the tier. Its titles sell individually for thousands, with some of its most iconic prints going for tens of thousands secondhand:

  • Arion’s latest edition of Alice in Wonderland cost $2,100 on its site, but it’s already sold out with only 230 copies printed.
  • One book from the press’s 1979 run of Moby-Dick is currently selling for $25,000 at Book Alley in Pasadena, CA.

Old-school fans. Last year, the company sold out of its annual subscriptions for the first time. Its backers include megawealthy tech vets like Salesforce co-founder Parker Harris; Caitlin Kalinowski, a robotics expert who has worked at OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic; and several private equity bigwigs.—MM

items.title: For 4 hours, all US flights ground to a halt
items.summary: Thiago Trevisan/Adobe Stock From just before 4pm ET until 8:15pm, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop, which halted all planes departing in the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the second…
items.author: Holly Van Leuven
items.contentHtml:
From just before 4pm ET until 8:15pm, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop, which halted all planes departing in the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the second time since 9/11 that a national ground stop went into effect.

What went down

At a White House press conference just after the ground stop was lifted, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the incident stemmed from new technology upgrades “overwhelming” the aging air traffic control communication system and did not appear to be the result of a cyberattack or anything “nefarious.” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said of those upgrades, “I didn’t anticipate that we would have an outage like this.”

Duffy also urged Congress to allocate $50 billion to fix the aging system and warned that more disruptions like this would happen unless the systems’ technical underpinnings were completely overhauled.

By 9:30pm ET, more than 6,600 flights had been canceled for Friday, and another 1,500 for Saturday:

  • Travel data firm Cirium estimated that 1.5 million travelers were stranded by the cancellations.
  • Sports teams ranging from college football to the NHL and NBA traveling for games were hard hit, and NFL teams had to wonder if their flights for weekend games would get jostled in the aftermath of the ground stop.
  • All air cargo and parcel shipment operations were also halted during the ground stop, impacting delivery times of consumer packages as well as supply chain logistics.

Lifting the ground stop helps get passengers moving again, but delays and cancellations are expected to carry into the weekend as planes, pilots, and crews are out of position.

Looking ahead: Duffy said that it was “going to be slow” to get air travel back to its baseline, but that he didn’t expect disruptions during Thanksgiving travel in a couple of weeks.—HVL

items.title: World recovers from the day Microsoft stood still
items.summary: Nick Iluzada Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services slowly began returning to normal yesterday, after the tech company’s massive outage disrupted business-as-usual around the world on Thursday, causing somewhat of a syllabus day for some workers, and leaving others to…
items.author: Molly Liebergall
items.contentHtml:
Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services slowly began returning to normal yesterday, after the tech company’s massive outage disrupted business-as-usual around the world on Thursday, causing somewhat of a syllabus day for some workers, and leaving others to resort to…fax machines.

The outage hit Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Copilot, cloud, and security software users in more than 70 countries and territories, according to the outage tracker Downdetector.

  • Government offices, public transit networks, retailers, banks, and countless companies were affected.
  • All in all, the outage could cost at least $7 billion in lost productivity from tens of millions of Microsoft users, according to a Michigan think tank.

“We are deeply sorry,” Microsoft said yesterday on X. The company noted “encouraging recovery progress,” but said that “intermittent issues” might continue.

It’s not clear why this happened

“This was a technical issue” unrelated to AI, with “no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity,” Microsoft said. The company referenced an “elevated load” and said it’ll share more information as it reviews the incident.

Zoom out: This is another reminder of why the modern economy’s reliance on hyperscalers can be risky, as one company’s technical difficulties can mess with an entire planet’s daily operations. Similar concerns arose when Cloudflare and Amazon Web Services crashed huge swaths of the internet last year.—ML
